Look at m0, m1, m8, m9: they form a square across the top and bottom rows (top and bottom touch), in the first two columns. B = 0 and C = 0 stay fixed, so this quad is B'C'. Next the four corners m0, m2, m8, m10: that quad is B'D'. Only m5 is left. Its only useful neighbour is m1, giving the pair m1, m5 where A = 0, C = 0, D = 1 and B changes, so A'C'D. Answer: F = B'C' + B'D' + A'C'D, seven literals instead of the original 28 in canonical form.

Worked example 3, the middle and the edges: If F = Σm(5, 7, 13, 15), all four 1s sit in the centre of the 4-variable map. B = 1 and D = 1 stay fixed, so F = BD. If instead F = Σm(4, 6, 12, 14), the 1s sit at the left and right edges of the two middle rows. They look far apart, but by wrap-around they form a quad. B = 1 and D = 0 stay fixed, so F = BD'. This is why you must always check the edges and corners before you settle on small groups.

Avoid redundant groups: Take F(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 3, 6, 7). You can see three pairs: m1 with m3 gives A'C, m3 with m7 gives BC, and m7 with m6 gives AB. But do we need all three? m1 and m3 are already covered by A'C, and m6 and m7 by AB. The middle group BC covers nothing new, so it is redundant. Minimum answer: F = A'C + AB. This is the consensus theorem from lesson 06 drawn as a picture: AB + A'C + BC = AB + A'C. A good habit is to ask of every circle, "does this cover at least one 1 that nobody else covers?" If not, erase it.

More than one right answer: Some maps have two equally good answers. Take F(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7). One minimum is A'B' + BC' + AC. Another is A'C' + B'C + AB. Both use three terms of two literals each, and both are correct. Here every 1 has two possible partners, so the map goes round in a circle. In an exam, either answer gets full marks if your groups are valid and minimal. Don't panic when your friend's answer looks different; check both with a few rows of the truth table.

A step-by-step strategy: One, draw the map with correct Gray labels and fill in the 1s. Two, find any 1 that can be grouped in only one way, especially lonely 1s, and circle those first. Three, look for the biggest possible groups: octets, then quads, then pairs, always checking wrap-around and corners. Four, cover each remaining 1 using the largest group that contains it. Five, remove redundant groups. Six, write one product term per group and OR them together. In the next lesson these ideas get proper names: prime implicants and essential prime implicants.

Filling the map from an expression: You don't always need the truth table first. Take F = A'B + AC' with three variables. The term A'B means every cell where A = 0 and B = 1. In the 3-variable map the rows are A only, so A'B is the top row cells where B = 1, which are m2 and m3. The term AC' is the bottom row cells where C = 0, which are m4 and m6. Shading a term's region directly is much faster than building a full truth table, and it trains your eye for reading groups backwards.

Real-life example 1, the debate judges: In a school debate competition in Chattogram, three judges each have a button. A green light should turn on when at least two judges press. Call the buttons A, B, C. The light is 1 for rows 011, 101, 110 and 111, so F = Σm(3, 5, 6, 7). On the 3-variable map, m7 sits in the middle of the bottom row with m3 above it, m5 to its left and m6 to its right. Three pairs: m3 with m7 gives BC, m5 with m7 gives AC, m6 with m7 gives AB. All three are needed, because each covers a 1 the others miss. So F = AB + AC + BC, the famous majority function, built with three 2-input AND gates and one 3-input OR gate.

Real-life example 2, a prime number toy: A kids' maths toy shows a number from 0 to 15 using four switches A, B, C, D, and a bulb lights if the number is prime. Primes here are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, so F = Σm(2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13). On the map, m2 can only pair with m3, giving A'B'C. m11 can only pair with m3, giving B'CD. m13 can only pair with m5, giving BC'D. m7 is still uncovered, and it can pair with m5 (A'BD) or with m3 (A'CD). Choose either. One minimum answer: F = A'B'C + B'CD + BC'D + A'BD. Four AND gates and one OR gate, instead of six 4-input AND gates.

Common mistakes: Writing columns as 00, 01, 10, 11 instead of Gray order. Forgetting that m3 and m2 swap places. Circling diagonals, L shapes, or groups of 3 or 6. Forgetting that edges and corners wrap. Making two small pairs when one quad was possible. Keeping a redundant group. Reading the term wrongly, for example keeping a variable that actually changes inside the group. A good final check is to count literals (a quad in a 4-variable map must give 2) and to test two or three rows of the truth table against your answer.

What exams ask: "Simplify F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(...) using a K-map and draw the circuit." "Why are K-map rows and columns labelled in Gray code?" "Show that the four corners of a 4-variable map form a group." "Find all minimal SOP expressions." Sometimes they give an expression instead of a minterm list, so you must plot it first. Practise with at least ten maps and the patterns will start to jump out at you, just like spotting your friend in a crowd at Sadarghat.

Limits and what comes next: K-maps are lovely up to four variables, still okay at five, and painful at six or more, because the adjacency is hard to see. In lesson 09 we add don't-care conditions, prime and essential prime implicants, product-of-sums answers from a K-map, and five-variable maps. In lesson 10 we learn the Quine-McCluskey method, a table-based recipe that a computer can follow for any number of variables.

Recap: A K-map is a truth table drawn in Gray order so that neighbouring cells differ in one variable. Adjacent 1s merge because X + X' = 1. Groups must be rectangles of size 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16, can wrap around edges and corners, should be as big and as few as possible, and may overlap. In each group, keep the variables that stay fixed and drop the ones that change. With this one picture you can turn long canonical forms into short, cheap circuits.
key_points: A K-map is a truth table drawn so that neighbouring cells differ in exactly one variable.
Rows and columns use Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10, so m3 sits before m2 and m7 before m6.
Adjacent 1s merge because XY + XY' = X; the changing variable disappears.
Groups are rectangles of 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells; edges and corners wrap around.
Make groups as large and as few as possible; overlaps are allowed; drop redundant groups.
In a group, keep variables that stay fixed (plain if 1, complemented if 0) and drop the ones that change.
A group of 2^k cells removes k variables; some maps have more than one minimal answer.
lessons.tip: Before every K-map, write the Gray labels 00, 01, 11, 10 and the cell numbers in pencil in the corner of each cell. Most K-map mistakes are placing a 1 in the wrong cell, not grouping badly.
lessons.task: On paper, simplify F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15) with a 4-variable K-map (hint: look at the corners and the centre). Then check your answer by testing three rows of the truth table.

quiz.q: Why are K-map columns labelled 00, 01, 11, 10 instead of 00, 01, 10, 11?
options: So that neighbouring cells differ in exactly one bit
So that m3 always comes first
quiz.explain: Gray order makes every pair of neighbours (including the wrap-around) differ in one variable, so they can be combined.

quiz.q: In a 4-variable K-map, a valid group of 4 cells gives a product term with how many literals?
quiz.explain: A group of 2^k cells removes k variables; 4 = 2^2, so 4 - 2 = 2 literals remain.

quiz.q: F(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 2, 4, 6) simplifies to:
quiz.explain: These are the first and last columns (BC = 00 and 10), which wrap around into one quad where only C = 0 stays fixed.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a legal K-map group?
options: The four corners of a 4-variable map
A pair that wraps from the left edge to the right edge
quiz.explain: Group sizes must be powers of two: 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16. Six is not allowed.

quiz.q: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(5, 7, 13, 15) simplifies to:
quiz.explain: These four cells sit in the centre of the map; B = 1 and D = 1 stay fixed, while A and C change.

lessons.title: K-Maps Deeper: Don't-Cares, Prime Implicants, POS and 5 Variables
lessons.content:
Imagine you order tea at a roadside tong stall and the cha-wala asks, "Sugar?" You say, "I don't care, whatever is easy." Now he has freedom. If the sugar pot is right in his hand he adds it; if not, he skips it. Either way you are happy. Digital design has the same kind of freedom. Sometimes certain input combinations never happen, or we simply don't care what the output is for them. These are called don't-care conditions, and a smart designer uses them to make K-map groups bigger and circuits smaller. This lesson takes K-maps from "I can circle some 1s" to the full university level: don't-cares, prime and essential prime implicants, product-of-sums answers, and five-variable maps.

Where we are: In lesson 08 you learned the basic 2, 3 and 4-variable K-maps, Gray order, wrap-around and the grouping rules. Here we add the proper vocabulary and a reliable procedure, so you can prove your answer is minimal instead of hoping. Lesson 10 will turn the same ideas into a table method that a computer can run.

Don't-care conditions: A don't-care is an input combination for which the output is not specified. There are two common reasons. One, the combination can never occur. For example, a BCD digit uses 4 bits but only the codes 0000 to 1001 (0 to 9) are valid, so inputs 1010 to 1111 (10 to 15) never appear. Two, the combination can occur but nobody looks at the output then, for example a display that is switched off. In a truth table or K-map we write a don't-care as X (some books use d or a dash). In a function we list them separately: F = Σm(1, 3) + d(5, 7).

How to use don't-cares: Treat each X as a joker card. If an X helps you make a group bigger, pretend it is 1 and include it. If it does not help, pretend it is 0 and leave it out. You never have to cover an X, and you must never make a group that contains only X's, because that would add a useless term. Small example: F(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 3) + d(5, 7). Without the X's, m1 and m3 form a pair A'C. With the X's, m1, m3, m5 and m7 form a quad (the whole C = 1 half of the map), so F = C. One literal instead of two, just by using the freedom we were given.

Implicant: Now the vocabulary. An implicant of F is a product term that is 1 only where F is 1 (or don't-care). On a K-map, any valid rectangle of 1s (and maybe X's) is an implicant. A single minterm is an implicant too. Implicants are all the "legal circles" you could draw.

Prime implicant: A prime implicant (PI) is an implicant that cannot be made any bigger. If you try to double the rectangle in any direction, you hit a 0. On a K-map, a prime implicant is a group that is not completely inside another larger legal group. For example, in a map where m5, m7, m13 and m15 are all 1, the pair m5, m7 is an implicant but not prime, because it sits inside the quad BD. The quad BD is prime if it cannot grow into an octet.

Essential prime implicant: An essential prime implicant (EPI) is a prime implicant that covers at least one 1 which no other prime implicant covers. That 1 has only one way to be covered, so this PI must be in every minimum answer. Important: the special 1 must be a real 1, not a don't-care. A don't-care never makes a PI essential, because we don't have to cover it.

The reliable procedure: Step one, find all prime implicants: for each 1, find the largest groups that contain it. Step two, mark the essential ones: look for 1s that sit inside exactly one prime implicant. Step three, include all essential PIs in the answer and tick off every 1 they cover. Step four, cover the remaining 1s with as few extra prime implicants as possible, preferring larger ones. This is exactly the method lesson 10 uses in table form.

Worked example of PIs: Simplify F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15). Plot the 1s. The prime implicants are: BD (cells 5, 7, 13, 15), B'D' (the four corners 0, 2, 8, 10), CD (3, 7, 11, 15), B'C (2, 3, 10, 11), AD (9, 11, 13, 15) and AB' (8, 9, 10, 11). Six quads, all prime. Now find essentials. Cell m5 lives only in BD, so BD is essential. Cell m0 lives only in B'D', so B'D' is essential. Together they cover 0, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15. Still uncovered: 3, 9, 11.

Finishing the example: m3 can be covered by CD or B'C. m9 can be covered by AD or AB'. No single prime implicant covers both 3 and 9 (they differ in two bits, A and C, and the quad joining them would need m1, which is 0). So we need two more terms. One minimum answer is F = BD + B'D' + CD + AD. Other choices like BD + B'D' + B'C + AB' are equally minimal: four terms, two literals each. This example shows why the procedure matters. If you had started by circling CD and AD, you might later miss that BD and B'D' were compulsory and end up with extra terms.

Product of sums from a K-map: Sometimes the POS form is cheaper, or the question asks for it. The trick: group the 0s instead of the 1s. Grouping 0s with the same rules gives an SOP expression for F', the complement. Then apply De Morgan's theorem to get F as a product of sums. A shortcut that gives the same result: for each group of 0s, write a sum term in which a variable that stays 0 appears plain and a variable that stays 1 appears complemented. That is the maxterm rule from lesson 07, just applied to bigger groups.

Worked POS example: Take F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 1, 2, 5, 8, 9, 10) from lesson 08. Its SOP minimum was B'C' + B'D' + A'C'D, which has 7 literals. The 0s are at 3, 4, 6, 7, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. Group them: AB covers 12, 13, 14, 15; CD covers 3, 7, 11, 15; BD' covers 4, 6, 12, 14. So F' = AB + CD + BD'. Apply De Morgan: F = (A' + B')(C' + D')(B' + D). That is only 6 literals, one fewer than the SOP answer. So always check both forms when cost matters; the cheaper one wins.

Don't-cares in POS: When you group 0s, a don't-care can be treated as 0 if it helps. Note that the same X may be used as 1 in your SOP answer and as 0 in your POS answer. That is fine. The two answers then differ only on don't-care rows, which by definition nobody cares about. They are both correct implementations of the specification.

Five-variable maps: With A, B, C, D, E there are 32 cells. The common way, used in Morris Mano's textbook, is to draw two 4-variable maps side by side: the left one for A = 0 (minterms 0 to 15) and the right one for A = 1 (minterms 16 to 31), each with rows BC and columns DE in Gray order. Inside each map the usual adjacency holds. Across the two maps, a cell is adjacent to the cell in the same position in the other map, because they differ only in A. A group that appears identically in both maps loses A and doubles in size. Some books draw the 5-variable map as one wide 4 by 8 mirrored grid; the cells are the same, only the picture differs, so follow the style your teacher uses.

Worked 5-variable example: Simplify F(A, B, C, D, E) = Σm(0, 2, 4, 6, 9, 13, 21, 23, 25, 29, 31). In the A = 0 map, cells 0, 2, 4, 6 have B = 0 and E = 0 with C and D changing, giving A'B'E'. Cells 9 and 13 (A = 0) and 25 and 29 (A = 1) sit in the same positions in both maps; they all have B = 1, D = 0, E = 1, giving the quad BD'E. Finally 21, 23, 29, 31 in the A = 1 map have C = 1 and E = 1, giving ACE. So F = A'B'E' + BD'E + ACE, three terms instead of eleven five-literal minterms.

Six or more variables: A 6-variable map needs four 4 by 4 maps, and adjacency stretches across all of them. It is possible but slow and very error-prone. Real designers stop using K-maps around here. Lesson 10's tabular method, and software tools, take over.

Real-life example 1, a rooftop water pump: Many Dhaka buildings have a rooftop tank and a pump. Say the tank has a low-level sensor L (1 when water reaches it) and a high-level sensor H (1 when water reaches the top), plus a manual switch M. The pump should run when the tank is below L, or when the caretaker turns M on and the tank is not full. H = 1 with L = 0 is impossible, since water can't reach the top without passing the low sensor. With variables in order H, L, M, the function is F = Σm(0, 1, 3) + d(4, 5). Using the two X's, cells 0, 1, 4, 5 form a quad L'. Cell 3 pairs with 1 to give H'M. So F = L' + H'M. Without the don't-cares you would get H'L' + H'M, one literal more.

Real-life example 2, rounding taka: A shop's billing circuit rounds an amount to the nearest ten taka. It looks at the last digit, stored in BCD as A B C D, and outputs 1 (round up) when the digit is 5 or more. So F = Σm(5, 6, 7, 8, 9) + d(10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15). Using the don't-cares, the whole A = 1 half (8 to 15) is an octet: A. Cells 5, 7, 13, 15 give BD, and cells 6, 7, 14, 15 give BC. Answer: F = A + BD + BC, only 5 literals. Without the don't-cares the best you can do is AB'C' + A'BD + A'BC, which is 9 literals. Same job, almost half the hardware.

Common mistakes: Making a group of only X's. Thinking every X must be covered. Calling a PI essential because of a don't-care. Calling every big group essential without checking whether another PI also covers its 1s. In POS, forgetting to complement: grouping 0s gives F', not F. Writing the POS sum term with the wrong polarity (in a 0-group, a variable that is 1 appears complemented). In 5-variable maps, joining cells across the two halves that are not in the same position.

What exams ask: "Simplify F = Σm(...) + d(...) in SOP and POS and compare the cost." "Define implicant, prime implicant and essential prime implicant with an example." "List all prime implicants and identify the essential ones." "Simplify this 5-variable function." "Design a BCD circuit using don't-cares." Show your groups clearly and label each with its term; examiners give marks for the steps.

Recap: Don't-cares (X) are free choices: use them as 1 when they enlarge a group, ignore them otherwise, and never group them alone. A prime implicant is a group that cannot grow; an essential prime implicant covers some 1 that no other prime implicant covers, so it is always in the answer. For POS, group the 0s to get F', then use De Morgan. Five-variable maps are two 4-variable maps where cells in the same position are neighbours. With these tools you can find, and defend, a truly minimal circuit.
key_points: Don't-cares (X) are inputs that never occur or whose output doesn't matter; written F = Σm(...) + d(...).
Use an X as 1 only when it enlarges a group; never make a group of only X's.
An implicant is any valid group; a prime implicant cannot be made bigger.
An essential prime implicant covers a real 1 that no other prime implicant covers, so it is in every minimum answer.
Procedure: find all PIs, take the essentials, then cover remaining 1s with as few PIs as possible.
For POS, group the 0s to get F', then apply De Morgan; compare SOP and POS cost.
A 5-variable map is two 4-variable maps; cells in the same position in both are adjacent.
lessons.tip: When you hunt for essential prime implicants, go 1 by 1 and ask, "How many prime implicants contain this cell?" Write the number in the cell. Every cell marked 1 points straight at an essential prime implicant.
lessons.task: A BCD digit (A B C D) is given. Design a circuit that outputs 1 when the digit is odd and greater than 4 (that is 5, 7 or 9). Use don't-cares for 10 to 15, find the minimum SOP and the minimum POS, and compare their literal counts.

quiz.q: How should a don't-care (X) be treated in a K-map?
options: As 1 only if it makes a group bigger, otherwise ignored
It must be covered by its own group
quiz.explain: Don't-cares are free choices: include them when they help enlarge a group; never group them alone.

quiz.q: An essential prime implicant is:
options: A prime implicant that covers at least one 1 no other prime implicant covers
Always the largest group on the map
A group made only of don't-cares
quiz.explain: If some 1 can only be covered by this prime implicant, it must appear in every minimum answer.

quiz.q: To get a POS expression from a K-map, you group:
quiz.explain: Grouping 0s gives F' in SOP form; complementing with De Morgan gives F in POS form.

quiz.q: In a 5-variable map drawn as two 4-variable maps (A = 0 and A = 1), which cells are adjacent across the two maps?
options: Cells in the same position in both maps
Cells in the same row only
No cells are adjacent across maps
quiz.explain: Cells in the same position differ only in A, so they are neighbours.

quiz.q: F(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 3) + d(5, 7). The minimum SOP is:
quiz.explain: Using both don't-cares, cells 1, 3, 5, 7 form the quad where C = 1.

lessons.title: The Quine-McCluskey (Tabular) Method
lessons.content:
Imagine the class teacher hands you a pile of 200 exam scripts and says, "Find every pair of students whose roll numbers differ by exactly one digit." Staring at the whole pile won't work. Instead you sort the scripts into small stacks first, then compare only stacks that could possibly match, ticking off scripts as you go. That is the spirit of the Quine-McCluskey method. A K-map relies on your eyes spotting neighbours. Quine-McCluskey (QM for short), also called the tabular method, replaces the eyes with a step-by-step table that never gets confused, works for any number of variables, and can be written as a computer program.

A bit of history: The philosopher and logician Willard Van Orman Quine described the idea of prime implicants in the early 1950s, and Edward McCluskey turned it into a practical tabular procedure in 1956. Together the method carries both names. It gives an exact minimum two-level SOP, which is why textbooks still teach it even though modern tools use faster methods for huge circuits.

Why we need it: A K-map is great for up to four variables and okay for five. At six variables you juggle four maps, and beyond that the picture method collapses. Also, a computer can't "see" rectangles. QM gives a recipe: list, sort, compare, tick, repeat. Each step is simple bit comparison, which is exactly what a computer is good at, and also something you can do neatly on paper in an exam.

The one rule behind it: QM uses the same rule as the K-map: XY + XY' = X. Two terms that differ in exactly one bit combine, and that bit is replaced by a dash (-) to show the variable has been eliminated. For example 0010 (A'B'CD') and 1010 (AB'CD') differ only in A, so they combine into -010, which means B'CD'. Later, terms that already contain dashes can combine again, but only if their dashes are in exactly the same positions and they differ in exactly one other bit.

Step 1, list and group by the number of 1s: Write every minterm (and every don't-care) in binary. Then sort them into groups by how many 1s they contain. This number is called the index. Why bother? Two terms that differ in one bit must have indexes that differ by exactly one. So you only ever need to compare a group with the very next group. That saves a huge amount of useless checking, just like comparing only neighbouring stacks of scripts.

Running example: Simplify F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 1, 2, 8, 10, 11, 14, 15). In binary: 0 = 0000 has zero 1s. 1 = 0001, 2 = 0010 and 8 = 1000 have one 1. 10 = 1010 has two. 11 = 1011 and 14 = 1110 have three. 15 = 1111 has four. So the groups are: index 0: {0}; index 1: {1, 2, 8}; index 2: {10}; index 3: {11, 14}; index 4: {15}.

Step 2, first round of combining: Compare every term in one group with every term in the next group. Whenever two terms differ in exactly one bit, write the combined term with a dash, list which minterms it came from, and put a tick next to both originals. From the example: 0 with 1 gives 000- (0, 1). 0 with 2 gives 00-0 (0, 2). 0 with 8 gives -000 (0, 8). From index 1 to 2: 1 = 0001 and 10 = 1010 differ in three bits, so no. 2 with 10 gives -010 (2, 10). 8 with 10 gives 10-0 (8, 10). From index 2 to 3: 10 with 11 gives 101- (10, 11); 10 with 14 gives 1-10 (10, 14). From index 3 to 4: 11 with 15 gives 1-11 (11, 15); 14 with 15 gives 111- (14, 15). Every original minterm got ticked, so none of them is prime on its own.

Step 3, keep combining: Now take the new list of pairs, again grouped by index, and repeat. The rule is stricter: the dashes must be in the same position. 00-0 (0, 2) and 10-0 (8, 10) have the dash in the same place and differ only in the first bit, so they give -0-0 (0, 2, 8, 10). -000 (0, 8) and -010 (2, 10) give the same -0-0 again; write it once only. 101- (10, 11) and 111- (14, 15) give 1-1- (10, 11, 14, 15), and so do 1-10 and 1-11. The pair 000- (0, 1) has its dash at the end, and no pair in the next group has a dash there, so it cannot combine. It stays unticked.

Step 4, stop and collect: Try combining -0-0 with 1-1-. Their dashes are in different positions, so no. Nothing more can combine, so we stop. Every term that never got a tick is a prime implicant. Here we have three: 000- which is A'B'C' (covers 0, 1), -0-0 which is B'D' (covers 0, 2, 8, 10), and 1-1- which is AC (covers 10, 11, 14, 15). To read a dashed term, go position by position A, B, C, D: a 1 gives the plain variable, a 0 gives the complement, and a dash means the variable is gone.

Step 5, the prime implicant chart: Now we pick the smallest set of prime implicants that covers every minterm. Draw a table: one row per prime implicant, one column per minterm of F, and put an X where a prime implicant covers that minterm. Important: don't-cares are NOT columns in this chart. They were only helpers during combining; we don't need to cover them.

Reading the chart: Look for columns with exactly one X. The prime implicant in that row is essential. In our example, column 1 has an X only in the A'B'C' row, so A'B'C' is essential. Columns 2 and 8 have an X only in B'D', so B'D' is essential. Columns 11, 14 and 15 have an X only in AC, so AC is essential. Together the three essentials cover all eight minterms. Final answer: F = A'B'C' + B'D' + AC. You can draw the K-map to confirm it; you will get exactly these three groups.

When essentials are not enough: Often, after you take the essential prime implicants and cross out the columns they cover, some columns remain. Then you choose among the remaining prime implicants. Two helpful ideas: if one row covers everything another row covers (and costs no more), the smaller row can be deleted, which is called row dominance. If a column has X's in every row where another column has X's, the bigger column is automatically covered and can be removed, which is called column dominance. Applying these simplifications can expose new essentials.

Petrick's method: For hard charts there is an exact algebraic trick by Stanley Petrick. Give each prime implicant a name P1, P2, and so on. For every remaining minterm, write an OR of the prime implicants that cover it. AND all these sums together, multiply out using Boolean algebra, and simplify with X + XY = X. Each product term in the result is a valid cover; pick the one with the fewest prime implicants, then the fewest literals.

Petrick worked example: Take F(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7). QM gives six prime implicants, all pairs: P1 = A'B' (0, 1), P2 = A'C' (0, 2), P3 = B'C (1, 5), P4 = BC' (2, 6), P5 = AC (5, 7), P6 = AB (6, 7). Every minterm is covered by exactly two of them, so there is no essential prime implicant at all; the chart is called cyclic. Petrick's product is (P1 + P2)(P1 + P3)(P2 + P4)(P3 + P5)(P4 + P6)(P5 + P6). The first two factors simplify to P1 + P2P3 by the distributive law. Multiplying everything out, the cheapest products are P1P4P5 and P2P3P6. So F = A'B' + BC' + AC or F = A'C' + B'C + AB, the same two answers we found on the K-map in lesson 08.

Don't-cares in QM: Include don't-cares in Step 1 and use them freely when combining, because they can help terms grow. But leave them out of the chart columns. Also, a prime implicant that covers only don't-cares is useless; just drop it. This matches the K-map rule: use X's to enlarge groups, but never group X's alone.

QM as a program: The steps fit nicely into code. In plain pseudo-code: terms = minterms + dontcares; repeat { for each pair (a, b) in neighbouring index groups: if dashes match and a, b differ in one bit then add merge(a, b) to next and mark a, b used; primes += unused terms; terms = next } until next is empty; then build the chart over minterms only and choose a cover. A student can write this in Python in an afternoon. The weak point is size: the number of prime implicants can grow exponentially with the number of variables, and choosing the minimum cover is an NP-hard problem, so for big real circuits tools use smart heuristics instead, such as the Espresso minimizer.

Real-life example 1, a factory controller: Suppose a garments factory in Gazipur wants a safety light for a cutting machine with six inputs: two hand buttons, a guard-door switch, a foot pedal, an emergency stop and a maintenance key. The engineer writes the truth table of 64 rows. A 6-variable K-map would need four 4 by 4 maps and careful cross-checking. With QM, the engineer can put the minterms in a spreadsheet, sort by number of 1s, and combine column by column, or simply run a short script. The answer is guaranteed minimal, and every step can be checked by a colleague.

Real-life example 2, tools you can use today: Free educational software such as Logisim Evolution has a combinational analysis window where you type a truth table and it shows a minimized expression and even builds the circuit. Professional FPGA and chip design tools also minimize logic automatically during synthesis, using much more advanced algorithms. But the ideas inside them, combining terms that differ in one bit, prime implicants and choosing a cover, are exactly what you learned in this lesson. When you understand QM, those tools stop being magic boxes.

K-map versus QM: K-maps are fast and visual for up to four or five variables and are perfect for exams and quick sketches. QM is slower by hand but systematic, works for any number of variables, handles don't-cares neatly, and is easy to program. Both give the same minimum answers, because both are built on the same prime implicant idea. Use the K-map to check small QM problems, and use QM when the map gets too big.

Common mistakes: Combining terms whose dashes are in different positions. Comparing groups that are not next to each other. Forgetting to tick the terms that combined, so you later mistake them for prime implicants. Writing the same combined term twice and treating it as two prime implicants. Putting don't-cares as columns in the chart. Stopping the combining too early. Reading dashed terms wrongly, for example treating a dash as a 0. Keep your tables neat with minterm lists in brackets; that alone prevents most errors.

What exams ask: "Minimize F = Σm(...) + d(...) using the Quine-McCluskey method, showing all tables." "Construct the prime implicant chart and identify the essential prime implicants." "Use Petrick's method to find all minimum solutions." "Compare the tabular method with the K-map method." The marks usually go to the grouping table, each combining round, the list of prime implicants, the chart, and the final expression, so show every stage.

Recap: Quine-McCluskey is the K-map turned into a table. Write minterms and don't-cares in binary, group by number of 1s, combine neighbouring groups when terms differ in one bit (dashes in the same places), tick what combines, and repeat. Unticked terms are prime implicants. Build a chart over the real minterms, take the essential prime implicants, and choose the rest by dominance or Petrick's method. It is slower by hand but exact, works for any size, and is the foundation of computer logic minimization.
key_points: Quine-McCluskey is a step-by-step table method that finds an exact minimum SOP for any number of variables.
Write minterms and don't-cares in binary and group them by the number of 1s (index).
Combine terms from neighbouring groups that differ in exactly one bit; replace that bit with a dash.
Later rounds combine only terms whose dashes are in the same positions; tick everything that combines.
Unticked terms are prime implicants; build a chart with real minterms only (no don't-care columns).
Columns with a single X reveal essential prime implicants; finish with dominance or Petrick's method.
QM is easy to program but can blow up for many variables, so big tools use heuristics like Espresso.
lessons.tip: Always write the minterm list in brackets next to every combined term, like -0-0 (0, 2, 8, 10). It makes duplicates obvious, makes the chart quick to fill, and lets you check each step against a K-map.
lessons.task: Minimize F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 14) with the Quine-McCluskey method on paper: grouping table, combining rounds, prime implicants and chart. Then draw the K-map and check that you get the same answer.

quiz.q: In the first step of Quine-McCluskey, minterms are grouped by:
options: The number of 1s in their binary form
quiz.explain: Grouping by the number of 1s (index) means only neighbouring groups need to be compared.

quiz.q: When can 10-0 and 00-0 be combined?
options: Only if they are in the same group
Now, because the dashes match and they differ in one bit, giving -0-0
quiz.explain: Dashes are in the same position and only the first bit differs, so they merge into -0-0.

quiz.q: At the end of the combining steps, the terms that never got a tick are:
quiz.explain: A term that could not be combined further cannot grow, so it is a prime implicant (not necessarily essential).

quiz.q: How are don't-cares used in the Quine-McCluskey method?
options: They become columns in the prime implicant chart
They are used while combining but are not columns in the chart
quiz.explain: Don't-cares help terms grow, but they don't need to be covered, so they are left out of the chart.

quiz.q: Petrick's method is used when:
options: The function has only one minterm
Essential prime implicants do not cover everything and a minimum choice among the rest is needed
You want to draw a K-map
quiz.explain: Petrick's method writes the covering condition as a product of sums and multiplies out to find all minimum covers, e.g. for cyclic charts.

lessons.title: NAND/NOR Implementation and Multilevel Logic
lessons.content:
Imagine a toy shop that sells only one kind of LEGO brick, a plain 2x4 brick. At first that sounds limiting. But with enough of those bricks you can still build a house, a car or a boat. NAND gates and NOR gates are like that single brick. Each one alone can build any logic circuit you want. Chip factories love this, because making one kind of gate again and again is cheaper and faster than making many kinds. In this lesson we learn how to turn any simplified expression into a circuit made only of NAND gates or only of NOR gates, and we look at circuits with more than two levels and at XOR-based parity circuits.

Where we are in the course: In earlier lessons you learned gates, Boolean algebra, canonical forms and K-maps. A K-map gives you a simplified sum of products (SOP) or product of sums (POS). That expression is like a recipe. Now we cook it with real gates, and real chips often prefer NAND and NOR.

Why NAND and NOR are popular: In CMOS technology, a NAND gate or NOR gate needs fewer transistors than an AND or OR gate. A 2-input NAND uses 4 transistors, while a 2-input AND is usually built as a NAND followed by an inverter, so it uses 6. NAND is also usually faster than NOR in CMOS, because its pull-up transistors are in parallel. So NAND is the favourite brick in many chips.

Universal gates, quick reminder: A gate is called universal if you can build NOT, AND and OR from it alone, because with those three you can build anything. With NAND: NOT A = (A·A)', which is a NAND with both inputs tied together. AND = NAND followed by NAND-as-inverter: ((AB)')' = AB. OR uses De Morgan: (A'·B')' = A + B, so you invert each input with a NAND and then NAND them. NOR works the same way in mirror form: NOT A = (A + A)', OR = NOR followed by an inverter, AND = (A' + B')' = AB.

Two-level logic: A two-level circuit has one level of gates feeding a second level. SOP is naturally AND-OR: the first level makes product terms with AND gates, the second level ORs them. POS is naturally OR-AND. We usually assume complemented inputs like A' are available for free, so inverters on the inputs are not counted as a level. Two-level circuits are fast because every signal passes through at most two gates.

The magic trick for SOP to NAND-NAND: Take F = AB + CD. Apply double complement: F = ((AB + CD)')'. By De Morgan, (AB + CD)' = (AB)'·(CD)'. So F = ((AB)'·(CD)')'. Look closely: (AB)' is a NAND of A and B. (CD)' is a NAND of C and D. And the outer part is a NAND of those two outputs. So an AND-OR circuit becomes a NAND-NAND circuit by simply replacing every gate with NAND. Same wiring, same inputs.

Why it works in pictures: A NAND gate is the same thing as an OR gate with bubbles (inverters) on its inputs. That is De Morgan in drawing form: (XY)' = X' + Y'. So in the NAND-NAND circuit, the second NAND is really an OR with input bubbles, and those bubbles cancel the output bubbles of the first-level NANDs. Two bubbles on one wire cancel, like saying "not not". This "bubble pushing" idea is the cleanest way to convert circuits.

One detail with single literals: Suppose F = AB + C'. The term C' goes straight into the OR gate. In a NAND-NAND version, the second-level NAND expects inverted signals, so a single literal must be complemented before entering. C' becomes C. So F = ((AB)'·C)'. Check: by De Morgan that is (AB)'' + C' = AB + C'. Correct. Rule: a single literal feeding the second level is complemented, or passed through a NAND used as an inverter.

Worked SOP to NAND example: Let F(A,B,C) = Σm(1, 3, 6, 7). From a K-map, F = A'C + AB. Level 1: NAND1 = (A'C)', NAND2 = (AB)'. Level 2: F = (NAND1 · NAND2)'. Three NAND gates in total, plus one inverter for A' if A' is not available, which itself can be a NAND with inputs tied. Let us test the row A=1, B=1, C=0: NAND1 = (0·0)' = 1, NAND2 = (1·1)' = 0, F = (1·0)' = 1. The truth table says m6 is 1. Good.

POS to NOR-NOR: The mirror trick works for POS. Take F = (A + B)(C + D). Double complement gives F = (((A + B)(C + D))')' = ((A + B)' + (C + D)')'. Now (A + B)' is a NOR, (C + D)' is a NOR, and the outer part is a NOR of those. So OR-AND becomes NOR-NOR by replacing every gate with NOR. A single literal entering the second level is again complemented.

Worked POS to NOR example: F = (A + B')(B + C). Level 1: N1 = (A + B')', N2 = (B + C)'. Level 2: F = (N1 + N2)'. Test A=0, B=1, C=0: N1 = (0 + 0)' = 1, N2 = (1 + 0)' = 0, F = (1 + 0)' = 0. Original: (0 + 0)(1 + 0) = 0·1 = 0. Matches.

The other two-level forms: There are 16 ways to pair two gate types, and 8 of them reduce to a single SOP or POS form. The useful ones: AND-OR, NAND-NAND, OR-NAND and NOR-OR all make SOP. OR-AND, NOR-NOR, NAND-AND and AND-NOR all make POS. The AND-OR-INVERT (AOI) form, F = (AB + CD)', and OR-AND-INVERT (OAI) form are sold as single complex gates in CMOS libraries because they are compact. To build AOI, find the SOP of F' (group the zeros in the K-map), then invert.

Multilevel logic: Two levels are fast but sometimes use many gates. Factoring can reduce gate count at the cost of more levels. Example: F = AC + AD + BC + BD needs four 2-input ANDs and a 4-input OR. Factor it: F = (A + B)(C + D). Now you need only two ORs and one AND. That is three gates instead of five. The trade-off is speed vs size. Each extra level adds a propagation delay, so designers balance them.

Converting multilevel circuits to NAND: Use bubble pushing. Draw the circuit with AND and OR gates. Replace each AND with a NAND (an AND with an output bubble). Replace each OR with an "invert-OR" (an OR with input bubbles, which is a NAND). Then look at every wire: if it has one bubble at one end and one bubble at the other, they cancel. If a wire has only one bubble, insert an inverter (a NAND with tied inputs) or complement the input literal. Done. For NOR-only, do the mirror: OR becomes NOR, AND becomes "invert-AND", which is a NOR.

Multilevel NAND example: F = A(CD + B) + BC'. Level by level: CD is an AND, then OR with B, then AND with A, then OR with BC'. That is four levels alternating AND, OR, AND, OR. Because they alternate nicely, replace all with NANDs. The single literal B entering the inner OR must be inverted, so feed B' there. The output is correct after checking bubbles. Alternating AND-OR levels is the easy case; when two ANDs sit in a row, you need an extra inverter between them.

XOR and XNOR: XOR, written A ⊕ B = A'B + AB', is 1 when the inputs differ. XNOR is its complement, 1 when they are equal. XOR can be built from four NAND gates: let X = (AB)'; then A ⊕ B = ((A·X)' · (B·X)')'. Try A=1, B=0: X = 1, (A·X)' = 0, (B·X)' = 1, output = (0·1)' = 1. Right, the inputs differ.

Odd function: XOR with many inputs, A ⊕ B ⊕ C, is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1. That is why multi-input XOR is called the odd function. Its K-map looks like a checkerboard, and no two 1-cells are adjacent, so a K-map cannot simplify it at all. In SOP, a 3-input XOR needs four 3-literal terms. With XOR gates it needs only two 2-input XORs. That is a big saving and a classic exam point.

Parity generator: Remember the parity bit from the codes lesson. For even parity on a 3-bit message x, y, z, the parity bit is P = x ⊕ y ⊕ z. Then the four bits together always have an even number of 1s. Example: message 101 has two 1s. P = 1 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 1 = 0. Total 1s = 2, even. Good.

Parity checker: The receiver XORs all four bits: C = x ⊕ y ⊕ z ⊕ P. If C = 0, no error was detected. If C = 1, an odd number of bits flipped. If a 0 changes to 1 during sending, the message 1010 with parity becomes, say, 1110, then C = 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ 0 = 1, error. A single parity bit cannot detect two flipped bits, because the count stays even.

Real life example 1, a cheap chip shop in Dhaka: Imagine a small electronics workshop in Elephant Road that builds a buzzer alarm for a shop door. The logic is "buzz if the door is open and the alarm is armed, or if the panic button is pressed": F = DA + P. The shop has a bag full of 7400 chips. The 7400 is a classic TTL chip with four 2-input NAND gates in one package. With NAND-NAND: N1 = (DA)', F = (N1 · P')'. They need P' too, so a third NAND with tied inputs inverts P. Three gates, one chip, no need to buy AND or OR chips. That is exactly why universal gates matter in practice.

Real life example 2, mobile data and error checks: When your phone sends data over Wi-Fi or mobile networks, every frame carries error-checking bits. Simple serial links like old UART connections between a microcontroller and a GPS module can use a single parity bit made by an XOR chain. Modern networks use stronger codes such as CRC, which is also built from XOR gates and shift registers. So the humble XOR gate is guarding your bKash payment message as it travels.

Common mistakes: Students often forget to complement single literals that go straight to the second level of a NAND-NAND or NOR-NOR circuit. Another mistake is converting SOP directly into NOR-NOR; that does not work. NOR-NOR naturally implements POS, so first get the POS (group zeros in the K-map). Some students also count input inverters inconsistently; read the question: if complemented inputs are not available, you must add inverters. Finally, do not try to simplify XOR functions with K-maps; recognise the checkerboard and use XOR gates.

What exams ask: Typical questions are "Implement F = Σm(...) using only NAND gates", "Implement the POS using NOR gates only", "Show that NAND is universal", "Draw a 3-bit even parity generator and a 4-bit checker", and "Convert this multilevel circuit to NAND only using bubble pushing". Always draw the AND-OR version first, then convert. Show one test row to prove it works.

Recap: NAND and NOR are universal gates and cheap in CMOS. SOP becomes NAND-NAND and POS becomes NOR-NOR by replacing every gate, while complementing single literals at the second level. Multilevel circuits save gates by factoring but add delay, and bubble pushing converts them. XOR builds the odd function and parity generators and checkers, which K-maps cannot simplify. Next we use these skills to design whole combinational circuits.
key_points: NAND and NOR are universal: each can build NOT, AND and OR alone.
In CMOS a 2-input NAND needs 4 transistors; NAND is the usual building brick.
SOP (AND-OR) becomes NAND-NAND by replacing every gate with NAND.
POS (OR-AND) becomes NOR-NOR by replacing every gate with NOR.
A single literal feeding the second level must be complemented.
Bubble pushing converts multilevel circuits: two bubbles on one wire cancel.
Multi-input XOR is the odd function; it makes parity generators and checkers and cannot be simplified by K-map.
lessons.tip: Always draw the plain AND-OR (or OR-AND) circuit first, then convert gate by gate and check one input row by hand. Converting straight from the expression in your head is where most mistakes happen.
lessons.task: Take F(A,B,C) = Σm(1, 3, 6, 7). Simplify it with a K-map, draw the AND-OR circuit, then redraw it using only NAND gates. Finally test all 8 input rows on paper and confirm the outputs match the minterm list.

quiz.q: Replacing every gate in a two-level AND-OR circuit with NAND gives:
quiz.explain: By double complement and De Morgan, NAND-NAND equals AND-OR.

quiz.q: NOR-NOR two-level circuits naturally implement:
quiz.explain: OR-AND (POS) becomes NOR-NOR by replacing every gate.

quiz.q: In a NAND-NAND circuit for F = AB + C', what enters the second-level NAND for the single term?
quiz.explain: A single literal entering the second level is complemented, so C' becomes C.

quiz.q: Even parity bit P for the message 1101 is:
quiz.explain: 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 1 = 1, so P = 1 makes the total count of 1s even.

quiz.q: Why can't a K-map simplify a 3-input XOR?
options: Its 1-cells form a checkerboard with no adjacent pairs
quiz.explain: The odd function puts 1s in a checkerboard pattern, so no groups can form.

lessons.title: Combinational Circuits: Analysis, Design and Code Converters
lessons.content:
Think of a vending machine at a Dhaka railway station that only checks which buttons are pressed right now. Press "tea" and it gives tea. It does not care what you pressed five minutes ago. A circuit that works like this, where the outputs depend only on the current inputs, is called a combinational circuit. It has no memory. In this lesson we learn the two big skills for these circuits: analysis, which means reading a circuit and finding what it does, and design, which means starting from a wish and building the circuit. Then we build two classic examples: a BCD to excess-3 code converter and a 7-segment display decoder.

What a combinational circuit is: It has n input variables, m output variables, and a network of logic gates in between. For every one of the 2^n input combinations, each output has one fixed value. So the whole behaviour can be written as a truth table with 2^n rows, or as m Boolean functions. There are no feedback loops and no flip-flops. Later in the course, sequential circuits will add memory, and they will contain combinational parts inside them.

Combinational vs sequential in one line: Combinational output = f(present inputs). Sequential output = f(present inputs, stored state). An adder is combinational. A counter is sequential, because it remembers where it is.

Analysis procedure, step by step: You are given a circuit diagram and asked "what does it do?" Step 1: make sure it is combinational, meaning no feedback paths from an output back to an input of an earlier gate. Step 2: label the output of every gate that is fed by inputs only, say T1, T2, and write their Boolean expressions. Step 3: label the gates fed by those, and write their expressions in terms of inputs and earlier labels. Step 4: keep going until you reach the outputs. Step 5: substitute to get each output as a function of the inputs only. Step 6: optionally make a truth table to see the behaviour and recognise it.

Analysis example: A circuit has inputs A, B, C. Gate 1 is an XOR: T1 = A ⊕ B. Gate 2 is an XOR: S = T1 ⊕ C. Gate 3 is an AND: T2 = AB. Gate 4 is an AND: T3 = T1·C. Gate 5 is an OR: Co = T2 + T3. Make the truth table. For A=1, B=1, C=0: T1 = 0, S = 0, T2 = 1, T3 = 0, Co = 1. For A=1, B=0, C=1: T1 = 1, S = 0, T2 = 0, T3 = 1, Co = 1. After all 8 rows you notice S is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1, and Co is 1 when at least two inputs are 1. This is a full adder, which we study next lesson. Analysis lets you recognise a circuit you never saw before.

Truth table approach to analysis: Instead of algebra, you can push each input row through the gates directly and fill a table with columns for A, B, C, T1, T2, T3 and outputs. For small circuits this is often faster and less error-prone than algebra.

Design procedure, step by step: This is the more important skill. Step 1: from the word specification, decide the number of inputs and outputs. Step 2: give them letter names. Step 3: build the truth table that defines how outputs relate to inputs. Step 4: write each output as a simplified Boolean function, using K-maps and don't-cares where some input combinations never happen. Step 5: draw the logic diagram, maybe converting to NAND or NOR. Step 6: verify by checking a few rows, or by simulation.

What practical design also cares about: Real designers care about the number of gates, the number of inputs per gate, the propagation delay through the longest path, the number of interconnections, and the limits of the chips they have. A circuit with the fewest gates is not always best if it is too slow.

Code converters: Different parts of a system sometimes use different codes for the same information. A code converter is a combinational circuit that takes one code and outputs another. Example: a calculator keypad gives BCD, but some arithmetic unit expects excess-3. A converter sits between them.

BCD to excess-3, the specification: Inputs are a BCD digit ABCD, where A is the most significant bit. Valid inputs are 0000 to 1001, decimal 0 to 9. Outputs wxyz are the excess-3 code, which is the BCD value plus 3. So 0 becomes 0011, 5 (0101) becomes 1000, and 9 (1001) becomes 1100. The input combinations 1010 to 1111 never occur, so they are don't-cares. That gives us 6 don't-care rows, which help a lot in simplification.

BCD to excess-3, the truth table in short: 0 → 0011, 1 → 0100, 2 → 0101, 3 → 0110, 4 → 0111, 5 → 1000, 6 → 1001, 7 → 1010, 8 → 1011, 9 → 1100. Now make a 4-variable K-map for each output with X in cells 10 to 15.

BCD to excess-3, the simplified answers: Output z is 1 for inputs 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, so z = D'. Output y is 1 for 0, 3, 4, 7, 8, so y = CD + C'D', which is the XNOR of C and D. Output x is 1 for 1, 2, 3, 4, 9, which simplifies to x = B'C + B'D + BC'D'. Output w is 1 for 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, which simplifies to w = A + BC + BD. Check digit 5 (A=0, B=1, C=0, D=1): z = 0, y = 0·1 + 1·0 = 0, x = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0, w = 0 + 0 + 1 = 1. Output 1000, which is 8 = 5 + 3. Correct.

Making it smaller with factoring: Notice x = B'(C + D) + B(C + D)'. That is x = B ⊕ (C + D). Also w = A + B(C + D). So the term (C + D) is shared, and you can build it once. This is multilevel logic from last lesson in action: fewer gates, a little more delay.

Binary to Gray code converter: Another classic. For 4-bit binary b3 b2 b1 b0, Gray code is g3 = b3, g2 = b3 ⊕ b2, g1 = b2 ⊕ b1, g0 = b1 ⊕ b0. So three XOR gates do the job. Example: binary 0110 (6) gives g3 = 0, g2 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1, g1 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0, g0 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1, Gray 0101. Going back, Gray to binary uses a chain: b3 = g3, b2 = b3 ⊕ g2, b1 = b2 ⊕ g1, b0 = b1 ⊕ g0.

The 7-segment display: Look at a digital clock or a microwave timer. Each digit is made of seven bars, called a to g. Segment a is the top bar, b the upper right, c the lower right, d the bottom, e the lower left, f the upper left, and g the middle. To show 8, all seven glow. To show 1, only b and c glow. A BCD to 7-segment decoder takes a BCD digit and outputs seven signals that turn on the right segments.

Common cathode vs common anode: In a common cathode display, all LED cathodes are joined to ground, and a segment glows when its input is 1. In a common anode display, all anodes are joined to the supply, and a segment glows when its input is 0, so the decoder outputs are active low. The classic 7447 chip drives common anode displays with active-low outputs, while the 7448 is meant for common cathode use.

Designing segment a: Segment a (the top bar) is on for digits 0, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and off for 1 and 4. With inputs A, B, C, D and don't-cares 10 to 15, the K-map gives a = A + C + BD + B'D'. Test digit 4 (0100): A = 0, C = 0, BD = 0, B'D' = 0, so a = 0, top bar off. Correct, the digit 4 has no top bar. Test digit 0 (0000): B'D' = 1, so a = 1. Correct.

Designing segment b: Segment b (upper right) is off only for digits 5 and 6. The K-map gives b = B' + C'D' + CD. Test 5 (0101): B' = 0, C'D' = 0, CD = 0, so off. Test 7 (0111): CD = 1, on. The other five segments are done the same way, each with its own K-map. Small detail: some displays draw 6 and 9 with or without a tail on segments a and d, so always follow the digit shapes given in the question.

Real life example 1, a bus fare display: The digital fare board on a modern Dhaka city bus or the token counter at a metro rail station shows numbers on 7-segment or matrix displays. Inside, a microcontroller usually stores a small lookup table, but the idea is identical to our decoder: digit in, segment pattern out. If you open a cheap Chinese digital clock from Gulistan market, you may even find a separate decoder chip doing exactly the BCD to 7-segment job.

Real life example 2, a rotary knob using Gray code: The volume knob on many car stereos and some sound systems is a rotary encoder. Some encoders output Gray code, because only one bit changes between neighbouring positions, so no wrong in-between reading happens. A small Gray to binary converter, just a chain of XOR gates, turns it into a normal binary number that the processor can use.

Common mistakes: Students forget to use the don't-cares in BCD problems and get much bigger expressions. Others treat don't-cares as zeros when making POS, or include a don't-care group that adds no real 1. A big one: confusing common anode and common cathode; with common anode, you need the complement of each segment function. In analysis, students sometimes skip labelling intermediate gates and get lost. Finally, always verify at least one row of your final circuit.

What exams ask: "Design a BCD to excess-3 code converter", "Design a BCD to 7-segment decoder for segment a (or e, or g)", "Analyse the given circuit and find its function", "Design a circuit that outputs 1 when a 4-bit input is a prime number" or "is divisible by 3", "Convert 4-bit binary to Gray code". The steps are always the same: truth table, K-maps with don't-cares, circuit, check.

Recap: A combinational circuit has no memory; outputs depend only on current inputs. Analysis labels every gate and derives output expressions or a truth table. Design goes specification, inputs and outputs, truth table, K-map simplification, circuit, verification. BCD to excess-3 uses six don't-cares and gives z = D', y = (C ⊕ D)', x = B ⊕ (C + D) and w = A + B(C + D). Binary and Gray converters are XOR chains. A 7-segment decoder needs one K-map per segment. Next, we design the most famous combinational circuits of all: adders.
key_points: Combinational circuit: outputs depend only on present inputs; no memory, no feedback.
Analysis: label gate outputs, derive expressions step by step, then build the truth table.
Design: spec, inputs and outputs, truth table, K-map simplification, circuit, verification.
Unused input codes (like BCD 1010 to 1111) are don't-cares and shrink the logic.
BCD to excess-3: z = D', y = (C ⊕ D)', x = B ⊕ (C + D), w = A + B(C + D).
Binary to Gray: g3 = b3, gi = b(i+1) ⊕ bi; Gray to binary is a running XOR chain.
7-segment decoder: one function per segment a to g; common anode needs active-low outputs.
lessons.tip: For any BCD design question, draw the K-map and write X in cells 10 to 15 before you put a single 1. That habit alone saves you from big, ugly expressions.
lessons.task: Write the digits 0 to 9 as 7-segment shapes on paper and mark which digits light segment g (the middle bar). Make the truth table and a K-map with don't-cares for 10 to 15, and find the simplest SOP for segment g.

quiz.q: What makes a circuit combinational?
options: Its outputs depend only on the present inputs
quiz.explain: Combinational circuits have no memory; outputs are a function of present inputs only.

quiz.q: In a BCD to excess-3 converter, what is the output for input 0101 (5)?
quiz.explain: Excess-3 is value + 3, so 5 + 3 = 8 = 1000.

quiz.q: Why are inputs 1010 to 1111 treated as don't-cares in BCD designs?
options: They never occur as valid BCD digits
quiz.explain: BCD only uses 0000 to 1001, so the other six combinations never appear.

quiz.q: Binary 1011 converted to Gray code is:
For a common anode 7-segment display, a segment glows when its input is:
quiz.explain: Common anode segments are active low: a 0 turns the LED on.

lessons.title: Adders and Subtractors
lessons.content:
Remember adding long numbers in class 3? You add the right column first, write the digit, and if the sum is 10 or more you carry 1 to the next column. Your teacher made you write that little carry above the next column. Computers do exactly the same thing, only in binary, and the "carry" is a wire running from one adding block to the next. Every time your phone adds two numbers, scrolls a page or calculates a bKash balance, adders are working underneath. In this lesson we build adders from the smallest piece upward, then turn an adder into a subtractor, detect overflow, and finally make addition faster with carry lookahead.

Binary addition reminder: In one column, 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 0 = 1, and 1 + 1 = 10, which means sum 0, carry 1. If there is also a carry coming in, 1 + 1 + 1 = 11, which means sum 1, carry 1. These four or eight cases are all we need to design adder circuits.

Half adder: A half adder adds two bits, A and B, and gives a sum S and a carry C. Truth table: 00 gives S=0, C=0; 01 gives S=1, C=0; 10 gives S=1, C=0; 11 gives S=0, C=1. You can read the functions straight off: S = A ⊕ B and C = AB. So a half adder is just one XOR gate and one AND gate. It is called "half" because it cannot accept a carry from a previous column.

Full adder: A full adder adds three bits: A, B and the carry-in Cin. It gives a sum S and a carry-out Cout. S is 1 when an odd number of the three inputs are 1, so S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin. Cout is 1 when at least two inputs are 1, which is the majority function: Cout = AB + ACin + BCin. A neat equivalent form is Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B). Check A=1, B=0, Cin=1: S = 1 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 1 = 0, Cout = 0 + 1·1 = 1. Indeed 1 + 0 + 1 = 2 = binary 10.

Full adder from two half adders: The first half adder adds A and B and gives P = A ⊕ B and G = AB. The second half adder adds P and Cin and gives S = P ⊕ Cin and a carry P·Cin. An OR gate combines the two carries: Cout = G + P·Cin. That matches the neat form above. So two half adders plus one OR gate make a full adder. Exams love asking you to draw this.

Ripple-carry adder: To add two 4-bit numbers A3A2A1A0 and B3B2B1B0, chain four full adders. The rightmost adds A0, B0 and C0 (usually 0). Its carry-out goes into the next adder as carry-in, and so on. The final carry-out C4 is the fifth bit of the result. Example: 0110 (6) + 0111 (7). Bit 0: 0 + 1 + 0 = 1, carry 0. Bit 1: 1 + 1 + 0 = 0, carry 1. Bit 2: 1 + 1 + 1 = 1, carry 1. Bit 3: 0 + 0 + 1 = 1, carry 0. Result 1101 = 13. Correct.

Why ripple adders are slow: Each full adder has to wait for the carry from the previous one. The carry "ripples" from right to left like a queue of people passing a message. In a common gate-level count, each stage adds about 2 gate delays to the carry path, so an n-bit ripple adder needs roughly 2n gate delays for the carry. For 4 bits that is fine, but for 64 bits it is far too slow for a modern processor.

Half subtractor: Subtracting A − B in one column: 0 − 0 = 0, 1 − 0 = 1, 1 − 1 = 0, and 0 − 1 = 1 with a borrow of 1 from the next column. So the difference D = A ⊕ B and the borrow Bo = A'B. Notice the difference is the same XOR as the sum; only the borrow differs from the carry.

Full subtractor: It computes A − B − Bin, where Bin is the borrow from the previous column. Difference D = A ⊕ B ⊕ Bin. Borrow-out Bout = A'B + A'Bin + BBin. Example A=0, B=1, Bin=1: we need 0 − 1 − 1. Borrow 2 from the next column: 2 − 1 − 1 = 0, so D = 0 and Bout = 1. Check with formulas: D = 0 ⊕ 1 ⊕ 1 = 0, Bout = 1·1 + 1·1 + 1·1 = 1. Good.

Subtraction using 2's complement: In practice nobody builds separate subtractors. Recall from the signed numbers lesson that A − B = A + (2's complement of B) = A + B' + 1. So subtraction is just addition with B inverted and an extra 1 added. Example in 4 bits: 7 − 5 = 0111 + 1010 + 1 = 0111 + 1011 = 1 0010. Drop the final carry and the answer is 0010 = 2.

The adder-subtractor circuit: Take a 4-bit ripple adder. Put an XOR gate on each B input, with the other XOR input connected to a control line M. Also connect M to C0. When M = 0: each XOR passes B unchanged (B ⊕ 0 = B), C0 = 0, so the circuit computes A + B. When M = 1: each XOR inverts B (B ⊕ 1 = B'), C0 = 1, so the circuit computes A + B' + 1 = A − B. One circuit, two jobs, controlled by one wire. This is how the ALU in a processor handles both ADD and SUB.

Unsigned results and the carry: For unsigned numbers, a final carry-out of 1 after addition means the result did not fit in n bits. For unsigned subtraction with this circuit, a carry-out of 1 means A ≥ B and the result is correct; a carry-out of 0 means A < B and the result is the 2's complement of the real negative answer.

Overflow for signed numbers: With signed 2's complement numbers in 4 bits, the range is −8 to +7. If you add 5 + 4 = 9, the answer does not fit. In binary, 0101 + 0100 = 1001, which looks like −7. That is overflow. Overflow can only happen when both numbers have the same sign and the result has the opposite sign. The circuit test is simple: V = C4 ⊕ C3, the XOR of the carry into the sign bit and the carry out of the sign bit. In 5 + 4: C3 = 1 (carry into bit 3), C4 = 0, so V = 1, overflow. In 7 − 5 above, C3 = 1 and C4 = 1, so V = 0, no overflow.

Carry lookahead: the idea: Instead of waiting for carries to ripple, compute every carry directly from the inputs. Define for each bit i: generate Gi = AiBi and propagate Pi = Ai ⊕ Bi. "Generate" means this column makes a carry by itself (1 + 1). "Propagate" means this column passes an incoming carry along (1 + 0 or 0 + 1). Then Ci+1 = Gi + PiCi.

Carry lookahead: expanding the equations: C1 = G0 + P0C0. C2 = G1 + P1C1 = G1 + P1G0 + P1P0C0. C3 = G2 + P2G1 + P2P1G0 + P2P1P0C0. C4 = G3 + P3G2 + P3P2G1 + P3P2P1G0 + P3P2P1P0C0. Each carry is now a two-level AND-OR expression of G, P and C0. So all carries appear after the same short delay: one level to make G and P, then two levels for the carries. The sums are Si = Pi ⊕ Ci. The price: the gates get bigger and wider for higher bits, so lookahead is usually done in groups of 4 bits.

Carry lookahead worked example: Add A = 1011 and B = 0110 with C0 = 0. G = A AND B bitwise: G3=0, G2=0, G1=1, G0=0. P = A XOR B: P3=1, P2=1, P1=0, P0=1. C1 = G0 + P0C0 = 0. C2 = G1 + P1C1 = 1. C3 = G2 + P2C2 = 0 + 1·1 = 1. C4 = G3 + P3C3 = 0 + 1·1 = 1. Sums: S0 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1, S1 = 0 ⊕ 0 = 0, S2 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0, S3 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0. Result C4 S = 1 0001 = 17. Check: 11 + 6 = 17. Correct.

Real chips: The classic 74283 chip is a 4-bit binary adder with fast internal carry. The 74182 is a lookahead carry generator that links several 4-bit blocks so that big adders stay fast. Modern processors use even fancier adder trees, but they are all built on the generate and propagate idea you just learned.

Real life example 1, a shop cash counter: A small shop in Mohammadpur uses a cheap electronic calculator to add a day's sales. Each time the shopkeeper presses plus, the calculator's chip adds the new amount to the running total. Inside, the numbers may be in BCD or binary, but the core is a chain of full adders with carries passing along, exactly like your class 3 column addition, just millions of times faster.

Real life example 2, a game score and overflow: Old video games stored scores in fixed-size registers. If a score is stored in 8 signed bits, its maximum is 127. Adding 1 more gives −128, a famous kind of bug where a score or a count "wraps around". Programmers in Bangladesh building apps today still meet the same issue when an int overflows, which is why understanding V = Cn ⊕ Cn−1 is not just exam theory.

Common mistakes: Students mix up the half adder carry (AB) with the half subtractor borrow (A'B). Others forget to set C0 = 1 in the adder-subtractor when subtracting. A very common exam error is checking overflow with the final carry alone; for signed numbers you must use C4 ⊕ C3, not just C4. And in carry lookahead, remember that Pi can be defined as Ai ⊕ Bi or as Ai + Bi for the carry equations, but the sum Si = Pi ⊕ Ci only works with the XOR version.

What exams ask: "Design a full adder and implement it using two half adders", "Design a full subtractor", "Draw a 4-bit adder-subtractor and explain the role of M", "Show the overflow detection logic", "Derive C1 to C4 for a carry lookahead adder", "Compare the delay of ripple-carry and carry lookahead adders", and short numerical additions in 2's complement with overflow checks.

Recap: A half adder gives S = A ⊕ B and C = AB. A full adder adds a carry-in too: S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin and Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B), and two half adders plus an OR make one. Chaining full adders gives a ripple-carry adder, simple but slow. XOR gates and a control line M turn it into an adder-subtractor using 2's complement. Signed overflow is detected by V = Cn ⊕ Cn−1. Carry lookahead uses Gi = AiBi and Pi = Ai ⊕ Bi to compute all carries in parallel. Next lesson: BCD adders, multipliers and comparators.
key_points: Half adder: S = A ⊕ B, C = AB.
Full adder: S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B); two half adders plus an OR gate.
Ripple-carry adder chains full adders; the carry delay grows with the number of bits.
Half subtractor: D = A ⊕ B, borrow = A'B; full subtractor adds a borrow-in.
Adder-subtractor: XOR each B with M and feed M into C0; M = 1 computes A + B' + 1 = A − B.
Signed overflow: V = Cn ⊕ Cn−1; it happens only when adding same-sign numbers.
Carry lookahead: Gi = AiBi, Pi = Ai ⊕ Bi, Ci+1 = Gi + PiCi, all carries computed in parallel.
lessons.tip: Keep a tiny table of carries above your binary additions, exactly like class 3. When you check overflow, circle the carry into the sign bit and the carry out of it; if they differ, it is overflow.
lessons.task: On paper, add 0111 and 0101 using four full adders drawn as boxes. Write every carry C1 to C4. Then compute 0111 − 0101 using the adder-subtractor with M = 1 and check the overflow bit V = C4 ⊕ C3 in both cases.

quiz.q: The carry output of a half adder is:
quiz.explain: The carry is 1 only when both bits are 1, so C = AB.

quiz.q: In a 4-bit adder-subtractor, what happens when M = 1?
options: B is inverted and C0 = 1, so it computes A − B
A is inverted, so it computes B − A
The output is forced to zero
quiz.explain: XOR with 1 inverts B, and C0 = 1 adds the 1 needed for 2's complement.

quiz.q: Signed overflow in an n-bit adder is detected by:
quiz.explain: Overflow happens when the carry into the sign bit differs from the carry out of it.

quiz.q: In carry lookahead, the generate signal Gi is:
quiz.explain: A column generates a carry by itself only when both bits are 1.

quiz.q: 4-bit signed: 0110 + 0011 gives 1001. What happened?
options: No overflow because there is no final carry
quiz.explain: Two positives gave a negative-looking result, so it is overflow.

lessons.title: BCD Adder, Binary Multiplier and Magnitude Comparator
lessons.content:
Picture a cashier at a supermarket like Shwapno. People think in decimal: 85 taka, 120 taka. The machine underneath thinks in binary. Sometimes a machine keeps numbers in BCD so that each decimal digit is stored separately and shown on a display without long conversions. Then it needs a special adder for BCD. The same cashier machine also multiplies prices by quantities and checks "is the payment greater than the bill?". In this lesson we build three combinational circuits that do exactly these jobs: a BCD adder, a binary multiplier and a magnitude comparator. All three are built from the adders and gates you already know.

Quick BCD reminder: In BCD (binary coded decimal), each decimal digit 0 to 9 is written as its own 4-bit binary code, 0000 to 1001. The decimal number 47 becomes 0100 0111. The codes 1010 to 1111 are never used. BCD wastes a few codes, but it makes decimal input and output easy, which is why calculators, digital meters and some financial systems like it.

The problem with adding BCD in binary: Add two BCD digits with a normal 4-bit binary adder. 3 + 4 = 0011 + 0100 = 0111 = 7. Fine. But 8 + 5 = 1000 + 0101 = 1101. That is 13 in binary, but 1101 is not a valid BCD digit. In BCD we want "carry 1, digit 3", which is 0001 0011. So whenever the binary sum is more than 9, we must correct it.

The correction rule: add 6: When the binary sum is greater than 9, add 0110 (decimal 6) to it, and the carry produced becomes the BCD carry. Why 6? Because a 4-bit binary group counts up to 16, but a decimal digit only to 10. The 6 skips the six unused codes. Example: 1101 + 0110 = 1 0011. Carry 1, digit 0011 = 3. That is 13. Correct.

When exactly to correct: Two BCD digits plus a carry-in can add up to at most 9 + 9 + 1 = 19. So the binary adder's output is a carry K and four bits Z8 Z4 Z2 Z1, with values 0 to 19. Correction is needed in two cases. Case 1: the binary adder produced a carry, K = 1 (sums 16 to 19). Case 2: there is no carry but the 4-bit sum is 10 to 15, which happens when Z8 = 1 and either Z4 or Z2 is 1. So the BCD carry is C = K + Z8Z4 + Z8Z2.

BCD adder block diagram: The circuit uses two 4-bit binary adders. The top adder adds the two BCD digits and the carry-in, giving K and Z8 to Z1. A small logic circuit computes C = K + Z8Z4 + Z8Z2. The bottom adder adds 0 C C 0 to the Z bits, which means it adds 0110 when C = 1 and 0000 when C = 0. The output of the bottom adder is the BCD sum digit, and C is the output carry to the next decimal digit. Any carry out of the bottom adder can be ignored, because C already holds the decimal carry.

BCD adder worked example: 9 + 9 + 1 (carry-in). Top adder: 1001 + 1001 + 1 = 1 0011, so K = 1, Z = 0011. C = 1 + 0 + 0 = 1. Bottom adder: 0011 + 0110 = 1001. So the digit is 9 with carry 1, the answer is 19. Correct. Another: 4 + 5 = 1001, K = 0, Z8 = 1 but Z4 = 0 and Z2 = 0, so C = 0. No correction. Digit 9. Correct.

Multi-digit BCD adders: To add two 3-digit decimal numbers like 275 + 348, connect three BCD adder stages, each passing its decimal carry C to the next. 5 + 8 = 13 gives digit 3, carry 1. 7 + 4 + 1 = 12 gives digit 2, carry 1. 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 gives digit 6. Answer 623. The structure is exactly like a ripple-carry adder, but each stage is one decimal digit.

Binary multiplication by hand: Binary multiplication is like decimal long multiplication, but easier, because each digit of the multiplier is 0 or 1. Multiply 11 (3) by 10 (2). Partial product 1: 11 × 0 = 00. Partial product 2: 11 × 1 = 11, shifted left one place. Add them: 00 + 110 = 110, which is 6. Each partial product bit is just an AND: aibj.

The 2-bit by 2-bit multiplier: Let A = A1A0 and B = B1B0. The product has 4 bits C3 C2 C1 C0. C0 = A0B0. The next column has two partial bits, A1B0 and A0B1; a half adder adds them, giving C1 and a carry. The third column has A1B1 plus that carry; a second half adder gives C2 and a carry, which is C3. So the circuit is 4 AND gates and 2 half adders. Test 11 × 11 (3 × 3): A0B0 = 1 so C0 = 1. A1B0 = 1, A0B1 = 1, half adder gives C1 = 0, carry 1. A1B1 = 1 plus carry 1, half adder gives C2 = 0, carry 1, so C3 = 1. Product 1001 = 9. Correct.

Bigger array multipliers: For a J-bit multiplier and a K-bit multiplicand you need J × K AND gates and (J − 1) adders, each K bits wide, and the product has J + K bits. For example, a 4-bit by 3-bit multiplier needs 12 AND gates and two 4-bit adders, and gives a 7-bit product. This "array multiplier" is a big grid of ANDs and adders. It is fast but uses lots of hardware. Processors often use smarter versions, but the partial-product idea stays the same.

Magnitude comparator: the job: A magnitude comparator compares two binary numbers A and B and gives three outputs: A > B, A = B and A < B. Exactly one of them is 1. A 4-bit comparator has 8 inputs, so its truth table would have 256 rows. That is too big for a K-map, so we design it by reasoning, which is a good lesson in itself: sometimes you design from the algorithm, not the table.

A small 2-bit comparator by K-map: For two 2-bit numbers A1A0 and B1B0 there are only 4 inputs and 16 rows, so a K-map works fine. Mark the cells where A > B: for example A = 10 and B = 01, or A = 11 and B = 10. Grouping them gives (A > B) = A1B1' + A0B1'B0' + A1A0B0'. Read it in words: A wins if its top bit is 1 and B's top bit is 0, or if B is 00 and A0 is 1, or if A is 11 and B0 is 0. Check A = 01, B = 00: the second term A0B1'B0' = 1, so A > B. Correct, 1 > 0. This K-map method is good for 2 bits, but for 4 bits the table explodes to 256 rows, which is why we switch to reasoning.

Equality: Two numbers are equal when every pair of bits is equal. Bit equality is an XNOR: xi = AiBi + Ai'Bi'. So (A = B) = x3 x2 x1 x0. Example: A = 1010, B = 1010: all xi = 1, so equal.

Greater than and less than: Compare from the most significant bit, just like you compare 5,281 and 5,263 by looking left to right until the digits differ. A > B if A3 = 1 and B3 = 0; or if bit 3 is equal and A2 = 1 and B2 = 0; and so on. So (A > B) = A3B3' + x3A2B2' + x3x2A1B1' + x3x2x1A0B0'. Mirror it for less than: (A < B) = A3'B3 + x3A2'B2 + x3x2A1'B1 + x3x2x1A0'B0.

Comparator worked example: A = 1011 (11), B = 1001 (9). Bit 3: both 1, x3 = 1. Bit 2: both 0, x2 = 1. Bit 1: A1 = 1, B1 = 0. So the third term x3x2A1B1' = 1, and A > B = 1. The less-than terms are all 0, and the equality output is 0 because x1 = 0. Correct, 11 > 9.

Cascading comparators: The classic 7485 chip is a 4-bit magnitude comparator with three cascade inputs. To compare 8-bit numbers, connect two of them: the low 4-bit chip's three outputs go into the cascade inputs of the high 4-bit chip. The high chip decides when the upper bits differ, and passes on the lower result when the upper bits are equal.

Real life example 1, a digital weighing scale in a bazar: Modern rice and fish shops in Kawran Bazar use electronic scales. The scale calculates price = weight × rate. Inside, a microcontroller multiplies binary numbers using partial products and adders, then often converts the result to decimal digits for the display. Some meters and older calculators keep the numbers in BCD all the way and use BCD adders, so each digit can go straight to a 7-segment decoder.

Real life example 2, a thermostat or water pump controller: Many homes in Dhaka have a water pump controller that switches the pump on when the tank level is below a set point and off when it is above another set point. At its heart is a comparison: is the measured value A greater than, equal to or less than the limit B? Simple controllers use a microcontroller instruction for that, but in hardware it is the same comparator logic: equality by XNOR and greater-than by checking from the top bit down.

Common mistakes: In BCD addition, students forget the case K = 1. 9 + 8 = 17 = 1 0001 in binary, and the 4-bit part 0001 looks valid, but the carry K = 1 means you must still add 6: 0001 + 0110 = 0111, digit 7, carry 1, answer 17. Another mistake is writing the correction condition as Z8Z4Z2 instead of Z8Z4 + Z8Z2. In multipliers, students forget that partial products shift left. In comparators, students forget the equality chain terms like x3x2 before A1B1'.

What exams ask: "Design a BCD adder and explain the correction logic", "Add 7 + 9 in BCD showing correction", "Design a 2-bit by 2-bit multiplier", "How many AND gates and adders are needed for a 4-bit by 3-bit multiplier?", "Design a 2-bit or 4-bit magnitude comparator and write the A > B expression", "Show how to cascade two 4-bit comparators".

Recap: A BCD adder adds two digits with a binary adder, then adds 0110 when the binary sum exceeds 9, using C = K + Z8Z4 + Z8Z2 as the decimal carry. A binary multiplier makes partial products with AND gates and sums them with adders; a 2×2 multiplier needs 4 ANDs and 2 half adders, and J × K bits need J × K ANDs and J − 1 K-bit adders. A magnitude comparator uses XNOR for equality and a top-down chain for greater and less. Next lesson: decoders and encoders, which select and name things.
key_points: BCD digits are 0000 to 1001; a binary sum above 9 must be corrected.
Correction: add 0110 when C = K + Z8Z4 + Z8Z2 is 1; C is also the decimal carry out.
A BCD adder uses two 4-bit binary adders and a small correction circuit.
Each partial product bit in binary multiplication is an AND: aibj.
2×2 multiplier: 4 AND gates and 2 half adders; J×K multiplier: J×K ANDs and J−1 K-bit adders.
Comparator equality: xi = XNOR(Ai, Bi) and (A = B) = product of all xi.
(A > B) = A3B3' + x3A2B2' + x3x2A1B1' + x3x2x1A0B0'; compare from the most significant bit.
lessons.tip: When adding in BCD, write the binary sum first and then ask two questions out loud: was there a carry? is the 4-bit sum above 9? If either answer is yes, add 6. Saying it aloud stops you from skipping the carry case.
lessons.task: Add 386 + 457 in BCD on paper. Write each digit in 4-bit BCD, add digit by digit, apply the +6 correction where needed and pass the decimal carries. Check that your answer is 843.

quiz.q: In a BCD adder, the output carry C equals:
quiz.explain: Correction is needed when there is a binary carry or the 4-bit sum is 10 to 15.

quiz.q: What do you add to correct a BCD sum greater than 9?
quiz.explain: Adding 6 skips the six unused 4-bit codes.

quiz.q: How many AND gates does a 4-bit by 3-bit array multiplier need?
quiz.explain: J × K = 4 × 3 = 12 partial product bits, one AND gate each.

quiz.q: For a 4-bit comparator, (A = B) is 1 when:
options: Any one bit pair is equal
quiz.explain: Equality needs x3x2x1x0 = 1, every bit pair equal.

quiz.q: A = 0110, B = 0101. Which output of the comparator is 1?
quiz.explain: Bits 3 and 2 match; at bit 1, A1 = 1 and B1 = 0, so A > B (6 > 5).

lessons.title: Decoders and Encoders
lessons.content:
Think of the room numbers in a university hall. A visitor walks in with a number like "305" and the guard points to exactly one room: third floor, fifth door. Out of hundreds of rooms, only one is chosen. That is what a decoder does with binary. You give it a binary number, and it switches on exactly one output line out of many. An encoder is the reverse: it looks at which line is active and tells you its number. These two blocks are everywhere: choosing memory chips, driving displays, reading keyboards.
