In this lesson we build them, add enable inputs, use decoders to make any Boolean function, and fix the weakness of simple encoders with a priority encoder.

What a decoder is: A decoder is a combinational circuit with n inputs and up to 2^n outputs. For each input combination, exactly one output is active. Because each output is 1 for exactly one input row, each output is simply one minterm of the inputs. That is the key idea: an n-to-2^n decoder is a minterm generator.

The 2-to-4 decoder: Inputs A and B, outputs D0 to D3. D0 = A'B', D1 = A'B, D2 = AB', D3 = AB. If A = 1 and B = 0, the input is 10 which is 2, so D2 = 1 and the rest are 0. The circuit is two inverters and four 2-input AND gates. Simple.

The 3-to-8 decoder: Inputs A, B, C (A most significant), outputs D0 to D7, with Di = mi. So D5 = AB'C, which is 1 only for input 101. It needs three inverters and eight 3-input AND gates. A common use is the binary to octal decoder: the 3-bit input picks one of eight octal digits.

Enable input: Real decoders have an extra input called enable, E. When E is active, the decoder works normally. When E is inactive, all outputs are inactive, no matter what A and B say. With an active-high enable, D0 = EA'B', D1 = EA'B and so on, so each AND gate just gets one more input. Enable lets you switch whole blocks on and off, which is very useful for building bigger decoders and for memory chip selection.

Active-low outputs: Many real decoder chips are built with NAND gates, because NAND is cheaper. Then the selected output goes to 0 and all others stay at 1. We call these outputs active low, and draw them with a bubble or write them with a bar. The classic 74138 is a 3-to-8 decoder with active-low outputs and three enable inputs, one active high and two active low. The 74139 contains two 2-to-4 decoders with active-low enables and outputs. Do not be scared by active-low signals: the logic is the same, only the meaning of 0 and 1 is swapped.

Building bigger decoders: Suppose you only have 3-to-8 decoders with enable, but you need a 4-to-16 decoder with inputs w, x, y, z. Feed x, y, z into both decoders. Connect w to the enable of the second decoder, and w' to the enable of the first. When w = 0, the first decoder is on and gives outputs D0 to D7. When w = 1, the second one is on and gives D8 to D15. Example: input 1010 has w = 1, so the second decoder works, and xyz = 010 selects its output 2, which is D10. Correct.

BCD to decimal decoder: Not every decoder uses all 2^n outputs. A BCD to decimal decoder has 4 inputs and only 10 outputs, D0 to D9, because BCD codes 1010 to 1111 never appear. Those six input combinations are don't-cares, so the AND gates can be smaller. For example, D9 only needs to check A and D: D9 = AD, because the only valid BCD code with A = 1 and D = 1 is 1001. The old 7442 chip is a BCD to decimal decoder with active-low outputs. Clever use of don't-cares makes this decoder cheaper than a full 4-to-16 one.

Implementing functions with a decoder: Since every output of a decoder is a minterm, any function written as a sum of minterms can be built by ORing the right decoder outputs. Take the full adder: S = Σm(1, 2, 4, 7) and C = Σm(3, 5, 6, 7). Use one 3-to-8 decoder with inputs x, y, z. One OR gate takes D1, D2, D4 and D7 to make S. Another OR gate takes D3, D5, D6 and D7 to make C. The whole full adder is one decoder and two 4-input OR gates.

A tip for many minterms: If a function has many minterms, it is cheaper to OR the minterms of its complement and then invert. If F has 6 out of 8 minterms, F' has only 2, so use a 2-input NOR of those two outputs. With active-low decoder outputs, ORing in active-low form becomes a NAND: F = NAND of the active-low outputs for F's minterms. So active-low decoder plus NAND gives the same function as active-high decoder plus OR.

What an encoder is: An encoder does the inverse of a decoder. It has 2^n (or fewer) input lines and n output lines. When one input is active, the output is the binary code of that input's number. Example: an octal to binary encoder has inputs D0 to D7 and outputs x, y, z. If D6 = 1, the output is 110.

Octal to binary encoder equations: Look at which inputs have a 1 in each output bit. x (the 4s bit) is 1 for D4, D5, D6, D7. y (the 2s bit) is 1 for D2, D3, D6, D7. z (the 1s bit) is 1 for D1, D3, D5, D7. So x = D4 + D5 + D6 + D7, y = D2 + D3 + D6 + D7 and z = D1 + D3 + D5 + D7. Just three OR gates, assuming exactly one input is active at a time.

The two problems of a simple encoder: Problem 1: if two inputs are active together, the output is garbage. D3 and D6 together give x = 1, y = 1, z = 1, output 111, which says "7", a line that is not even pressed. Problem 2: an output of 000 can mean either "D0 is active" or "nothing is active". The circuit cannot tell the difference. Both problems are solved by the priority encoder.

Priority encoder: A priority encoder gives each input a rank. If several inputs are active, the output is the code of the highest-priority one. It also has a valid output V, which is 1 when at least one input is active. Example: a 4-input priority encoder with D3 the highest priority. If D1 and D2 are both 1, the output is 10 for D2, ignoring D1. If no input is 1, V = 0 and the output bits are don't-cares.

Priority encoder truth table and equations: With inputs D0 to D3 and outputs x, y, V, the condensed truth table uses X for inputs that do not matter. Row "D3 = 1": output 11, whatever the others are. Row "D3 = 0, D2 = 1": output 10. Row "D3 = 0, D2 = 0, D1 = 1": output 01. Row "only D0 = 1": output 00. Simplifying with K-maps gives x = D2 + D3, y = D3 + D1D2' and V = D0 + D1 + D2 + D3. Check D1 = 1, D2 = 1, D3 = 0: x = 1, y = 0 + 1·0 = 0, output 10, that is D2. Correct, D2 beats D1.

Real chips: The 74148 is an 8-to-3 priority encoder with active-low inputs and outputs, plus enable-in and enable-out pins for cascading two of them into a 16-to-4 encoder. Interrupt controllers in computers use the same idea: when several devices ask the processor for attention at the same moment, the highest-priority request is served first.

Decoders in memory address selection: In a computer, the address bus carries a binary number. Higher address bits go into a decoder whose outputs drive the chip-select pins of memory chips. Exactly one memory chip is enabled for each address range. For example, with two address bits feeding a 2-to-4 decoder, four memory chips can each own one quarter of the address space. This "address decoding" is one of the most common real uses of decoders.

Decoder vs encoder side by side: A decoder goes from a small code to many lines, and each output is an AND (a minterm). An encoder goes from many lines to a small code, and each output is an OR of inputs. A decoder with n inputs has 2^n outputs; an encoder with 2^n inputs has n outputs. If you connect an encoder's output into a decoder, the line that was active on the encoder side becomes active again on the decoder side, which is how a few wires can carry a choice among many.

Real life example 1, a lift in a Dhaka apartment building: When you press button 5 in the lift, the panel must tell the controller "floor 5". The buttons are like encoder inputs and the controller receives a binary floor number. If two people press 3 and 7 at the same time, a priority scheme decides which call is handled first. On the other side, the floor indicator light at each landing works like a decoder output: the controller has the current floor as a binary number, and the decoder lights exactly one floor lamp.

Real life example 2, a simple keypad: A calculator or an old feature phone keypad has many keys but only a few wires to the processor. An encoder turns "key 9 pressed" into a short binary code. Real keypads use a scanning matrix of rows and columns, but the encoding idea is the same: many inputs, one small code. A priority rule handles the case when a child presses several keys at once.

Common mistakes: Students forget the enable input when drawing decoder-based circuits, or connect w to the wrong decoder when building a 4-to-16 decoder. Another mistake is mixing active-low and active-high outputs: with active-low outputs you must use NAND, not OR, to combine minterms. For encoders, students forget that a simple encoder gives wrong outputs for multiple active inputs and cannot distinguish D0 from no input; always mention V in a priority encoder. Finally, remember that a decoder output is a minterm and an encoder output bit is an OR of inputs.

What exams ask: "Design a 3-to-8 decoder with enable", "Build a 4-to-16 decoder from two 3-to-8 decoders", "Implement a full adder (or any function) using a decoder and OR gates", "Design an octal to binary encoder and state its limitations", "Design a 4-input priority encoder with a valid bit and write its equations". Draw the truth table first, then the circuit.

Recap: An n-to-2^n decoder activates exactly one output, and each output is a minterm, so a decoder plus OR gates can implement any function in canonical SOP. Enable inputs switch decoders on and off and let you build bigger decoders. Many chips use active-low outputs, so you combine them with NAND. An encoder is the inverse: one active input becomes a binary code built from OR gates. A priority encoder chooses the highest active input and adds a valid output. Next lesson: multiplexers, which select data instead of lines.
key_points: An n-to-2^n decoder activates exactly one output; each output is a minterm of the inputs.
Enable input: when inactive, all outputs are inactive; it lets decoders be combined and chip-selected.
Two 3-to-8 decoders plus enable make a 4-to-16 decoder (the top bit drives the enables).
Any function in Σm form = decoder + OR of its minterm outputs; full adder S = Σm(1,2,4,7), C = Σm(3,5,6,7).
Active-low decoder outputs are combined with NAND instead of OR.
Octal to binary encoder: x = D4+D5+D6+D7, y = D2+D3+D6+D7, z = D1+D3+D5+D7.
Priority encoder outputs the highest-priority active input and a valid bit V.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a decoder, say to yourself "minterm generator". Then any function question becomes easy: write the function as Σm, and wire those decoder outputs to one OR gate.
lessons.task: Using a 3-to-8 decoder drawn as a box, implement F(A,B,C) = Σm(0, 3, 5, 6). Then design a 4-input priority encoder on paper, fill its condensed truth table, and check the output when D0, D1 and D3 are all 1.

quiz.q: How many outputs does a 4-input decoder have?
quiz.explain: An n-to-2^n decoder with n = 4 has 2^4 = 16 outputs.

quiz.q: In a 3-to-8 decoder, which output is active for input 101?
quiz.explain: 101 in binary is 5, so D5 = AB'C is active.

quiz.q: A full adder's carry with a 3-to-8 decoder is the OR of which outputs?
quiz.explain: C = Σm(3, 5, 6, 7), the rows where at least two inputs are 1.

quiz.q: A simple octal to binary encoder outputs 000. What can you conclude?
options: Either D0 is active or no input is active
quiz.explain: Without a valid bit, 000 is ambiguous; a priority encoder adds V to fix this.

quiz.q: 4-input priority encoder (D3 highest): D0 = 1, D2 = 1, others 0. Output xy is:
quiz.explain: D2 has higher priority than D0, so the output is the code of D2, which is 10.

lessons.title: Multiplexers, Demultiplexers, Tri-State Buffers and Buses
lessons.content:
Imagine a TV with one screen and many channels. The remote control does not give you more screens; it chooses which channel reaches the one screen you have. A multiplexer, or MUX, is exactly that remote control in hardware. Many data inputs, one output, and a few select lines that decide which input gets through. A demultiplexer is the reverse: one input is sent to one of many outputs, like a postman delivering a letter to the right house. In this lesson we build MUXes and DEMUXes of different sizes, learn the clever trick of building any Boolean function with a MUX, and meet the tri-state buffer, which lets many devices share one wire called a bus.

What a multiplexer is: A multiplexer is a combinational circuit with 2^n data inputs, n select inputs and one output. The select lines carry a binary number, and the data input with that number is connected to the output. People also call it a data selector. A 4-to-1 MUX has 4 data inputs and 2 select lines; an 8-to-1 MUX has 8 data inputs and 3 select lines.

The 2-to-1 MUX: Data inputs I0 and I1, select S, output Y. If S = 0, Y = I0; if S = 1, Y = I1. As an equation, Y = S'I0 + SI1. The circuit: one inverter, two AND gates and one OR gate. Test S = 1, I0 = 0, I1 = 1: Y = 0·0 + 1·1 = 1, which is I1. Correct.

The 4-to-1 MUX: Inputs I0 to I3, selects S1 and S0, output Y = S1'S0'I0 + S1'S0I1 + S1S0'I2 + S1S0I3. Notice that each select combination is a minterm of S1 and S0, ANDed with one data input. So inside every MUX is a decoder: the select lines are decoded, and each decoder output opens one data gate. Example: S1S0 = 10 selects I2. If I2 = 1, the output is 1, whatever the other inputs are.

The 8-to-1 MUX and bigger: With 3 select lines, Y = Σ (mi · Ii) for i = 0 to 7, where mi is the minterm of S2S1S0. The classic 74151 chip is an 8-to-1 MUX with an enable (strobe) input and both Y and its complement as outputs. The 74153 contains two 4-to-1 MUXes and the 74157 contains four 2-to-1 MUXes sharing one select line. Bigger MUXes can be built as a tree: two 8-to-1 MUXes feeding a 2-to-1 MUX make a 16-to-1 MUX, with the top select bit controlling the final 2-to-1 stage.

Enable and quad MUXes: Like decoders, MUXes often have an enable input. When the enable is inactive, the output is forced to 0 (or to high impedance in some chips). A quad 2-to-1 MUX selects between two 4-bit numbers at once. For example, it can choose whether a 4-bit display shows the hours or the minutes, using one select line for all four bits.

The MUX as a universal function block: Here is the magic trick. Any Boolean function of n variables can be built with a 2^(n−1)-to-1 MUX and maybe one inverter. Use n − 1 variables as the select lines. For each select combination, the function depends only on the last variable, so the data input is one of four things: 0, 1, the last variable, or its complement.

MUX function example: Build F(x, y, z) = Σm(1, 2, 6, 7) with a 4-to-1 MUX. Use x and y as selects, z as the leftover. Group the truth table in pairs. xy = 00 covers m0 and m1; F is 0 for m0 (z = 0) and 1 for m1 (z = 1), so F = z, and I0 = z. xy = 01 covers m2 and m3; F is 1 for m2 (z = 0) and 0 for m3, so F = z', and I1 = z'. xy = 10 covers m4 and m5; F is 0 for both, so I2 = 0. xy = 11 covers m6 and m7; F is 1 for both, so I3 = 1. Done: one 4-to-1 MUX and one inverter for z'.

The implementation table method: For bigger functions, draw a small table. Columns are the data inputs I0 to I(2^(n−1)−1). Two rows: the top row lists minterms where the leftover variable is 0, the bottom row where it is 1. Circle the minterms of F. For each column: no circles gives 0, both circled gives 1, only the bottom circled gives the variable, only the top circled gives its complement. This method works for any function, and with an 8-to-1 MUX you can build any 4-variable function, which is very handy in exams.

A 4-variable example with an 8-to-1 MUX: Take F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(1, 3, 4, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15) with A, B, C on the selects and D left over. Look at the pairs. ABC = 000 holds m0 and m1; only m1 (D = 1) is in F, so I0 = D. ABC = 001 holds m2 and m3; only m3, so I1 = D. ABC = 010 holds m4 and m5; only m4 (D = 0), so I2 = D'. ABC = 011 holds m6, m7; neither, so I3 = 0. ABC = 100 holds m8, m9; neither, so I4 = 0. ABC = 101 holds m10, m11; only m11, so I5 = D. ABC = 110 and 111 hold m12 to m15, all in F, so I6 = I7 = 1. Check ABCD = 0100: the select is 010, I2 = D' = 1, and m4 is in F. Correct.

MUX or decoder for a function?: A decoder plus an OR gate needs one OR per output function, but it gives many functions of the same inputs almost for free, because all the minterms are already there. A MUX gives exactly one function, but it needs no extra OR gate and fits a 4-variable function in one 8-to-1 chip. So for one function, a MUX is usually smaller; for several functions of the same inputs, a decoder with a few OR gates is often better.

What a demultiplexer is: A demultiplexer takes one data input and sends it to one of 2^n outputs chosen by n select lines. All other outputs stay 0. A 1-to-4 DEMUX with data input E and selects S1 S0 has outputs D0 = S1'S0'E, D1 = S1'S0E, D2 = S1S0'E, D3 = S1S0E. If S1S0 = 11 and E = 1, then D3 = 1. If E changes to 0, D3 follows to 0. The data is routed, not changed.

Decoder with enable = demultiplexer: Compare the DEMUX equations with a 2-to-4 decoder with enable: D0 = EA'B' and so on. They are identical. Use the enable pin as the data input and the decoder's inputs as select lines, and the decoder is a demultiplexer. That is why chip catalogues often call a part a "decoder/demultiplexer", like the 74138 and 74139.

Time-division multiplexing: A MUX at one end and a DEMUX at the other, both driven by the same counting select lines, can send several signals over one wire by taking turns. First input 0 goes through, then input 1, and so on, very fast. The old telephone network used this idea, called time-division multiplexing, to carry many phone calls over one line. The receiver's DEMUX must stay in step with the sender's MUX.

Tri-state buffers: A normal gate output is always 0 or 1. A tri-state buffer has a third state: high impedance, written Z, where the output is effectively disconnected, as if the wire were cut. A tri-state buffer has a data input A, a control input C and an output Y. If C = 1, Y = A. If C = 0, Y = Z. Some tri-state buffers have active-low control, and some are inverting, so read the symbol carefully.

Why we need high impedance: If two ordinary outputs are wired together and one says 1 while the other says 0, they fight. Current flows from one to the other, the voltage is undefined and the chips can heat up or be damaged. With tri-state buffers, you can connect many outputs to one wire safely, as long as only one buffer is enabled at a time. All the others are in Z and simply do not take part.

Buses: A bus is a group of shared wires that many devices use to send data to each other. In a computer, the CPU, memory and input/output chips all sit on a data bus. Each device connects through tri-state buffers. A decoder is often used to make sure only one device's buffers are enabled at a time: its outputs drive the buffer controls, and since a decoder activates exactly one output, there is never a fight. A MUX can also be built this way: four tri-state buffers on one output line, with a 2-to-4 decoder driving their controls, act as a 4-to-1 MUX.

Real life example 1, a classroom projector switch: Many classrooms in Bangladeshi universities have a projector with an input switcher: HDMI 1 for the teacher's laptop, HDMI 2 for a student's presentation, VGA for an old PC. Pressing the source button changes the select value, and only that video signal reaches the projector. That is a multiplexer, just for video. The same pattern appears in a TV set-top box choosing channels and in a car stereo choosing between radio, USB and Bluetooth.

Real life example 2, the internal bus of a phone: Inside your phone, the processor talks to memory, the camera controller and other blocks over shared buses. Only one device drives the bus at a time, and the others keep their outputs disconnected. Modern chips often use multiplexer-based on-chip buses instead of real tri-state wires, but the rule "one talker at a time" is exactly the same. When people say a bus is "busy", they literally mean another device currently owns it.

Common mistakes: Students mix up the number of select lines: a 2^n-to-1 MUX has n select lines, so an 8-to-1 MUX has 3, not 8. In function implementation, students forget to use the leftover variable's complement, or choose the select variables in a different order from the table. Another frequent error is thinking a tri-state output of Z means 0; it does not, it means disconnected. And when building a 16-to-1 MUX from 8-to-1 MUXes, remember that the most significant select bit goes to the final stage.

What exams ask: "Design a 4-to-1 MUX using gates", "Implement F = Σm(...) using an 8-to-1 (or 4-to-1) MUX", "Build a 16-to-1 MUX from 4-to-1 MUXes", "Design a 1-to-4 DEMUX and show it is the same as a decoder with enable", "Explain tri-state buffers and why buses need them". Use the implementation table, and always write which variables are on the select lines.

Recap: A MUX selects one of 2^n data inputs using n select lines; Y = Σ mi Ii. MUXes come in 2-to-1, 4-to-1 and 8-to-1 sizes and can be built into trees. Any n-variable function fits in a 2^(n−1)-to-1 MUX with data inputs 0, 1, x or x'. A DEMUX routes one input to one of many outputs and is the same circuit as a decoder with enable. Tri-state buffers add a high-impedance state so many devices can share a bus, with only one enabled at a time. Next lesson: hazards and timing, where we find out what happens in the tiny moments when signals are still changing.
key_points: A 2^n-to-1 MUX has n select lines; Y = Σ (mi of the selects · Ii).
2-to-1 MUX: Y = S'I0 + SI1; every MUX contains a decoder of its select lines.
Any n-variable function fits a 2^(n−1)-to-1 MUX with data inputs 0, 1, x or x'.
Bigger MUXes are built as trees; the top select bit drives the last stage.
A DEMUX routes one input to one of many outputs; it is a decoder whose enable is the data input.
Tri-state buffer: output = input when enabled, high impedance Z when disabled.
A bus is shared wires; only one tri-state driver may be enabled at a time, often chosen by a decoder.
lessons.tip: For MUX function questions, always draw the two-row implementation table. It turns a confusing puzzle into four quick checks per column: none, both, bottom only, top only.
lessons.task: Implement F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0, 1, 3, 4, 8, 9, 15) using an 8-to-1 MUX with A, B, C on the select lines. Draw the implementation table, decide each data input (0, 1, D or D'), and test the rows ABCD = 0011 and 1111 on paper.

quiz.q: How many select lines does a 16-to-1 multiplexer need?
quiz.explain: 2^4 = 16, so 4 select lines.

quiz.q: F(x,y,z) = Σm(1,2,6,7) with a 4-to-1 MUX (selects x, y). What is I1?
quiz.explain: xy = 01 covers m2 (F=1, z=0) and m3 (F=0), so I1 = z'.

quiz.q: A 2-to-4 decoder with enable can act as which device?
quiz.explain: Use the enable as the data input and the inputs as selects; the equations match a DEMUX.

quiz.q: What does the high-impedance state Z of a tri-state buffer mean?
quiz.explain: Z means the buffer does not drive the wire at all, so others can use it.

quiz.q: Why must only one tri-state driver on a bus be enabled at a time?
options: To avoid two outputs fighting with different values
Because buses carry only one bit
quiz.explain: Two enabled drivers with different values would short and give an undefined voltage.

lessons.title: Hazards and Timing in Combinational Circuits
lessons.content:
Imagine a relay race at your school sports day. The baton has to pass from runner to runner, and each handover takes a moment. Now imagine two teams carrying two copies of the same message by different paths, one short and one long. For a short time, the person at the finish line has heard one message but not the other, and might shout the wrong answer. Logic gates are like those runners. Every gate takes a tiny time to react, and when a signal travels along two paths of different length, the output can flash a wrong value for a few nanoseconds. That flash is called a glitch, and the possibility of it is called a hazard. In this lesson we learn about propagation delay, find hazards, and remove them using a K-map.

Ideal vs real gates: Up to now we treated gates as perfect: the output changes the very instant the input changes. Real gates are made of transistors that need time to charge and discharge tiny capacitances. So the output always lags behind the input by a small delay. Truth tables describe the final, steady result, but not what happens during the change.

Propagation delay: The propagation delay of a gate is the time from an input change to the resulting output change. It is often measured between the 50 percent points of the input and output waveforms. There are two values: tPLH, the delay when the output goes from low to high, and tPHL, when it goes from high to low. They are often different. The average is tpd = (tPLH + tPHL) / 2. For old 7400-series TTL gates, typical delays were around 10 nanoseconds. Inside modern processors, a gate delay is far smaller, only a few picoseconds to tens of picoseconds.

Delay of a whole circuit: A circuit's delay is set by its slowest path from any input to any output, called the critical path. If an inverter, an AND gate and an OR gate each take 10 ns, a signal passing through all three takes 30 ns. That is the earliest time the output is guaranteed correct after an input change. Two-level circuits are popular partly because their critical path is short.

Things that change the delay: Delay depends on the gate type, the technology, the temperature, the supply voltage and the load. The number of gate inputs that one output drives is called fan-out; more fan-out means more capacitance to charge, and so more delay. Long wires also add delay. This is why the same circuit can be fast on one chip and slower on another.

Timing diagrams: A timing diagram draws each signal as a line against time, high for 1 and low for 0. To find a glitch, you draw the input change, then shift each gate's output by its delay. Where two shifted signals overlap in a bad way, you see a short pulse that the truth table never predicted. Drawing timing diagrams by hand is the best way to truly understand hazards.

What a hazard is: A hazard is a situation where a single input change can cause a temporary wrong output, because of different path delays. The wrong output is called a glitch. Whether the glitch actually appears depends on the exact delays, but a hazard means it is possible. There are two main kinds: static hazards and dynamic hazards.

Static-1 hazard: The output should stay at 1 before and after the input change, but it briefly drops to 0. This happens in sum-of-products (AND-OR) circuits. Static-0 hazard: The output should stay at 0, but it briefly jumps to 1. This happens in product-of-sums (OR-AND) circuits.

The classic static-1 example: Take F = AB + A'C. Let B = 1 and C = 1. Then F = A + A' = 1 for both A = 0 and A = 1. On paper, F stays 1 whatever A does. But look at the circuit. When A goes from 1 to 0, the term AB falls quickly to 0. The term A'C needs A' first, and A' comes from an inverter, so it rises a little later. For a moment, both AND outputs are 0, so the OR output dips to 0. With 10 ns per gate, the dip lasts about one inverter delay, around 10 ns. That is a static-1 hazard.

Seeing the hazard on a K-map: Draw the K-map of F = AB + A'C. The group for AB and the group for A'C are next to each other, but they do not overlap. The change of A moves us from a cell in one group to an adjacent cell in the other group. When a single variable change jumps between two adjacent 1-cells that are not covered by a common group, there is a static-1 hazard.

Removing the hazard: Add a redundant group that covers both adjacent cells. Here that is the consensus term BC. The new function is F = AB + A'C + BC. Logically BC adds nothing, because of the consensus theorem from the Boolean algebra lesson. But when B = 1 and C = 1, the BC gate stays at 1 the whole time A changes, holding the output up. The glitch is gone. The price is one extra AND gate and one more OR input.

Rule for hazard-free SOP: For every pair of adjacent 1-cells in the K-map, there must be at least one group that covers both. If two groups touch but do not overlap, add a bridging group. This removes static-1 hazards for single input changes. For POS circuits, apply the same rule to the 0-cells: every pair of adjacent 0-cells must share a group. For example, F = (A + B)(A' + C) has a static-0 hazard when B = 0 and C = 0, and adding the sum term (B + C) fixes it.

A second worked example: Take F(A,B,C) = Σm(0, 1, 5, 7). The minimal SOP is F = A'B' + AC: A'B' covers m0 and m1, and AC covers m5 and m7. Now check every adjacent pair of 1-cells. m0 and m1 sit in the same group, fine. m5 and m7 sit in the same group, fine. But m1 (001) and m5 (101) are adjacent, differing only in A, and they are in different groups. So with B = 0 and C = 1, changing A can cause a glitch. Add the bridging group B'C, which covers m1 and m5. The hazard-free form is F = A'B' + AC + B'C. Three terms instead of two, but the output is now steady during that change.

Dynamic hazard: Here the output should change once, from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0, but instead it changes three or more times, like 0 to 1 to 0 to 1, before settling. Dynamic hazards happen in multilevel circuits where the same input reaches the output along three or more paths with different delays. A good habit: if a multilevel circuit is free of static hazards, it is usually free of dynamic hazards too, so designers first remove static hazards by making the circuit hazard-free two-level logic.

Function hazards: If two or more inputs change at the same moment, the output may pass through an intermediate input combination with a different value. For example, if A and B change from 01 to 10 together, real wires will not change at exactly the same instant, so the circuit may briefly see 00 or 11. This kind is called a function hazard, and adding redundant terms cannot fix it. The practical fix is timing: wait until signals are stable before using the output.

When glitches matter: In a synchronous system, outputs are only sampled at the clock edge, after everything has settled. If the clock period is longer than the critical path delay, glitches are harmless, because nobody looks at the output during the flicker. Glitches matter in asynchronous circuits, in signals used as clocks or resets, in latches enabled by combinational logic, and in counters triggered by output edges. A glitch on a clock or reset line can make a flip-flop change state when it should not.

Worked timing example: Suppose an inverter, AND and OR each take 5 ns. In F = AB + A'C with B = C = 1, A falls at time 0. AB falls at 5 ns. A' rises at 5 ns, so A'C rises at 10 ns. The OR output reacts to AB falling at 10 ns, and to A'C rising at 15 ns. So F is low from 10 ns to 15 ns: a 5 ns glitch. With the BC term added, BC stays 1 all the time, and F never drops.

Real life example 1, a traffic signal at a Dhaka junction: Picture a simple traffic controller where the green light is driven by combinational logic from a few timer signals. If a glitch dropped the green signal for a few nanoseconds, the lamp would not visibly flicker, because a bulb or LED driver responds far more slowly. But if that same signal fed the clock input of a counter that counts cycles, the glitch could add a false count and mess up the timing for the whole junction. This is why designers keep glitchy signals away from clocks.

Real life example 2, a high-speed processor: In the processor of a laptop running at a few gigahertz, the clock period is well under one nanosecond. Every path between flip-flops must settle inside that time. Chip design tools perform static timing analysis, checking millions of paths to make sure the critical path fits. When a phone gets hot and the chip slows its clock, part of the reason is that delays grow at high temperature, so the chip must give its signals more time.

Common mistakes: Students think adding the consensus term changes the function; it does not, it only adds a redundant cover. Others look for static-1 hazards in POS circuits or static-0 hazards in SOP circuits; remember SOP circuits can have static-1 hazards, POS circuits static-0. Some forget that overlapping groups already protect the boundary, so not every adjacent pair needs a new term. And in timing diagrams, students often forget to delay each gate output separately.

What exams ask: "Define propagation delay, tPLH and tPHL", "Find the critical path delay of this circuit", "Explain static-1, static-0 and dynamic hazards with examples", "Show that F = AB + A'C has a hazard and remove it", "Given F = Σm(...), find a hazard-free SOP", and "Draw the timing diagram showing the glitch". Use the K-map and look at every boundary between groups.

Recap: Real gates have propagation delay, tPLH and tPHL, and a circuit's speed is set by its critical path. Unequal path delays cause hazards: static-1 in SOP, static-0 in POS, and dynamic hazards in multilevel circuits. In a K-map, a hazard appears where two adjacent 1-cells are not covered by a common group; adding the redundant consensus group removes it. Multiple simultaneous input changes cause function hazards that only timing can handle. Synchronous design hides most glitches by sampling after things settle. Next lesson we start sequential logic, where feedback gives circuits memory.
key_points: Propagation delay: time from input change to output change; tpd = (tPLH + tPHL) / 2.
The critical path (slowest input-to-output path) sets the circuit's speed.
Hazard: unequal path delays can cause a temporary wrong output called a glitch.
Static-1 hazards occur in SOP circuits; static-0 hazards occur in POS circuits.
K-map rule: adjacent 1-cells not covered by a common group signal a static-1 hazard.
Fix: add the redundant consensus term, e.g. F = AB + A'C + BC.
Dynamic hazards (multiple output changes) appear in multilevel circuits; function hazards come from simultaneous input changes.
lessons.tip: When you check for hazards, put your finger on every pair of side-by-side 1s in the K-map and ask "is there one loop around both?". If not, draw one. Physical pointing finds hazards faster than staring.

quiz.explain: PHL means propagation, high to low.

quiz.q: Which kind of hazard can occur in a two-level AND-OR (SOP) circuit?
quiz.explain: In SOP, the output can briefly drop to 0 while it should stay 1.

quiz.q: How do you remove the static-1 hazard in F = AB + A'C?
quiz.explain: BC covers the boundary between the two groups and holds the output at 1.

quiz.q: A dynamic hazard means the output:
options: Changes several times when it should change once
Changes only on a clock edge
quiz.explain: In a dynamic hazard, a single 0-to-1 or 1-to-0 change becomes something like 0-1-0-1.

quiz.q: Why are glitches often harmless in synchronous circuits?
options: Outputs are sampled at the clock edge after they settle
Flip-flops remove all hazards inside gates
quiz.explain: If the clock period exceeds the critical path delay, the output is stable when it is sampled.

lessons.title: Sequential Logic and Latches
lessons.content:
Think about a light switch on your wall. You press it once and the light stays on, even after you take your hand away. The switch remembers. Now think about a doorbell button: the bell rings only while your finger is on it. The doorbell is like the combinational circuits we have built so far, with outputs that depend only on what is happening right now. The wall switch is like a sequential circuit: its output depends on what happened before. In this lesson we cross a big bridge in the course. We learn how a circuit can remember one bit, using a trick called feedback, and we build the simplest memory cells: the SR latch, the gated SR latch and the D latch.

Combinational vs sequential: A combinational circuit's outputs are a function of its present inputs only. A sequential circuit's outputs depend on its present inputs and on its present state, which is information stored inside it from the past. Structurally, a sequential circuit is a combinational circuit plus memory elements, with some outputs of the memory fed back as inputs to the combinational part.

Synchronous vs asynchronous: In a synchronous sequential circuit, the memory elements change only at specific moments set by a clock signal, a steady square wave of pulses. In an asynchronous circuit, the state can change whenever the inputs change, with no clock. Synchronous circuits are much easier to design and test, so almost all modern digital systems, from your calculator to your phone's processor, are synchronous. Latches, which we learn today, are the basic building block for both.

The clock in brief: A clock is a signal that switches between 0 and 1 at a regular rate. Its period T is the time of one full cycle, and its frequency is f = 1/T. A 1 GHz clock has a period of 1 nanosecond. A 50 MHz clock has a period of 20 ns. Next lesson, flip-flops will use the clock's edges to decide exactly when to store data.

Feedback creates memory: Take two inverters and connect them in a loop: the output of the first goes into the second, and the output of the second goes back into the first. If the first output is 1, the second output is 0, which keeps the first output at 1. This is stable forever, as long as power is on. The opposite, first output 0, is also stable. A circuit with two stable states is called bistable, and it stores one bit. The trouble is that two plain inverters give no way to change the stored bit. We need inputs, so we replace the inverters with NOR or NAND gates.

The SR latch with NOR gates: Two NOR gates are cross-coupled: each gate's output goes into one input of the other gate. The free inputs are S (set) and R (reset), and the outputs are Q and Q'. Remember that a NOR gate outputs 0 if any input is 1. Set: S = 1, R = 0 forces Q' to 0, and then Q becomes 1. Reset: S = 0, R = 1 forces Q to 0, and then Q' becomes 1. Hold: S = 0, R = 0 keeps the previous state, because each gate just passes on what the other says. That is memory.

The forbidden input of the NOR latch: If S = 1 and R = 1 together, both NOR outputs become 0, so Q = Q' = 0, which breaks the rule that Q' is the complement of Q. Worse, if both inputs then go back to 0 at the same time, the latch may end up in either state, depending on tiny delay differences; it can even oscillate for a while. So S = R = 1 is called forbidden or not allowed for the NOR SR latch. Designers make sure it never happens.

SR latch function table: S R → Q next. 0 0 → Q (no change). 0 1 → 0 (reset). 1 0 → 1 (set). 1 1 → forbidden. Written as an equation with the condition SR = 0, the next state is Q+ = S + R'Q. Check: S = 0, R = 0 gives Q+ = Q. S = 1, R = 0 gives Q+ = 1. S = 0, R = 1 gives Q+ = 0. Correct.

Walking through the NOR latch in time: Start with Q = 0. Make S = 1 for a short pulse: Q' drops to 0 after one gate delay, then Q rises to 1 after another. Now return S to 0. Q stays 1, because the lower NOR sees Q' = 0 and R = 0, and keeps Q at 1. Later pulse R = 1: Q drops to 0, then Q' rises. Release R and Q stays 0. So a short pulse is enough to change the stored bit, and the latch keeps it afterwards.

The S'R' latch with NAND gates: Build the same cross-coupled structure with NAND gates. Since NAND gives 1 if any input is 0, the inputs work as active low. S' = 0 sets Q to 1, R' = 0 resets Q to 0, S' = R' = 1 holds, and S' = R' = 0 is forbidden, because it forces both outputs to 1. So the NAND latch is the mirror image of the NOR latch. Many textbooks draw bubbles on its inputs to show they are active low.

Switch debouncing, a real use: When you press a mechanical push-button, the metal contacts bounce a few times in a few milliseconds, producing several pulses instead of one clean change. If that signal drives a counter, one press might count as five. A simple fix uses an SR latch with a two-position switch: the first contact to touch the S side sets the latch, and the bounces, which only touch and leave that side again, do not change anything, because a latch in the set state stays set when S returns to 0. The output is one clean change.

The gated SR latch: Often we want the latch to listen to S and R only at certain times. Add an enable input En (sometimes called C or G). Two AND gates (or NAND gates in the usual NAND-based design) pass S and R to the latch only when En = 1. When En = 0, S and R are ignored and the latch holds its state. When En = 1, it behaves like a normal SR latch. The forbidden case S = R = 1 with En = 1 still exists, which is annoying.

The D latch: The D latch removes the forbidden case completely. It has one data input D and an enable En. Inside, D goes to the S input and D' (through an inverter) goes to the R input of a gated SR latch. Since S and R are always complements, S = R = 1 can never happen. When En = 1, Q follows D: if D = 1 then Q = 1, if D = 0 then Q = 0. When En = 0, Q holds the last value. The name D stands for data. Its characteristic equation is simply Q+ = D when enabled.

Transparency: When En = 1, the D latch is transparent: any change on D passes straight through to Q, after a small delay, like looking through a clear window. When En goes to 0, the window becomes a photograph: Q freezes at whatever D was at that moment. Example: En = 1, D goes 0 → 1 → 0 → 1; Q follows all of these. Then En drops to 0 while D = 1, and Q stays 1, no matter what D does next.

Why transparency is a problem: Suppose the output of a latch passes through some logic and comes back to its own D input, as in a counter. While En = 1, the new value of Q flows around the loop and changes D again, which changes Q again, and so on, possibly many times in one enable pulse. The final value depends on how long En stays high and on the gate delays. This is called a race. The fix is a storage element that changes only at one instant, the clock edge. That is the flip-flop, the topic of the next lesson.

Latches in real chips: The 7475 is a classic quad D latch chip. Latches are still used today: in some memory designs, in low-power circuits, and in input ports that capture data from a bus when a strobe signal is active. The basic cell of static RAM (SRAM) is also a bistable loop, a pair of cross-coupled inverters with access transistors, which keeps its bit as long as power stays on.

Real life example 1, a power cut and the fan regulator: In many Bangladeshi homes, when load-shedding ends and the power comes back, some electronic devices return to "off" while others resume their old setting. Devices that resume usually store their setting in non-volatile memory, but devices with only latch-type memory lose it, because a bistable loop needs power to hold its state. A latch is memory, but it is volatile memory: no power, no bit.

Real life example 2, a quiz buzzer at a school competition: In a school quiz contest, each team has a buzzer button. The first team to press should light its lamp and keep it lit, even after they let go. Each lamp can be driven by an SR latch: the button sets the latch, and the quizmaster's reset button clears all latches for the next question. Extra logic can block the other teams once one latch is set. It is a fun, real circuit you can actually build with a few NAND gates.

Common mistakes: Students mix up the NOR latch, whose forbidden input is S = R = 1, with the NAND latch, whose forbidden input is S' = R' = 0. Some think a latch needs a clock; a basic SR latch has none, and a gated latch only has an enable level, not an edge. Another common error is to say a D latch has a forbidden state; it does not. Finally, students confuse "transparent" with "broken": transparency is normal latch behaviour while enabled.

What exams ask: "Distinguish combinational and sequential circuits", "Draw an SR latch using NOR gates and explain its function table", "Why is S = R = 1 forbidden?", "Draw the NAND S'R' latch", "Design a D latch from a gated SR latch", "Draw the timing diagram of a D latch for given En and D waveforms", and "Explain how an SR latch debounces a switch".

Recap: Sequential circuits remember a state, built from feedback. Two cross-coupled inverters are bistable and hold one bit. The NOR SR latch sets with S = 1, resets with R = 1, holds with 00, and forbids 11; the NAND version is active low and forbids 00. A gated SR latch adds an enable, and a D latch removes the forbidden case: while enabled, Q follows D; when disabled, Q holds. Latches are transparent while enabled, which causes races in feedback circuits. Next lesson: edge-triggered flip-flops, which fix that.
key_points: Sequential output depends on inputs and stored state; feedback creates memory.
Synchronous circuits change state only at clock events; clock frequency f = 1/T.
NOR SR latch: S=1 sets, R=1 resets, 00 holds, 11 forbidden; Q+ = S + R'Q with SR = 0.
NAND S'R' latch is active low: 00 is forbidden, 11 holds.
Gated SR latch listens to S and R only while the enable is 1.
D latch: Q follows D while enabled and holds when disabled; no forbidden input.
Latches are transparent while enabled, which can cause races; flip-flops fix this with edges.
lessons.tip: Draw latch timing diagrams step by step, one gate delay at a time, writing Q and Q' after each step. The moment you can predict the forbidden-state mess by hand, latches will stop feeling like magic.
lessons.task: Draw a NOR SR latch on paper. Starting from Q = 0, apply this sequence of (S, R): (1,0), (0,0), (0,1), (0,0), (1,0). Write Q and Q' after each step. Then draw a D latch timing diagram where En is high for the first half of each cycle and D changes in the middle of each half.

quiz.q: In a NOR SR latch, which input combination is forbidden?
quiz.explain: S = R = 1 forces Q = Q' = 0 and leaves an unpredictable state afterwards.

quiz.q: In a NAND S'R' latch, what do S' = 1, R' = 1 do?
quiz.explain: NAND latch inputs are active low, so 1 and 1 means neither set nor reset is asked.

quiz.q: What happens to a D latch output when En = 0?
quiz.explain: With the enable off, the latch ignores D and keeps the stored bit.

quiz.q: Why does a D latch have no forbidden state?
options: S and R are always complements because R = D'
quiz.explain: D feeds S and D' feeds R, so S = R = 1 is impossible.

quiz.q: What does 'transparent' mean for a latch?
options: While enabled, input changes pass straight to the output
It changes only on clock edges
quiz.explain: While En = 1, Q follows D like looking through a clear window.

lessons.title: Flip-Flops: D, JK and T
lessons.content:
Think of a photo booth at a fair. While you are posing and moving around, nothing is saved. Then there is one flash, and exactly that instant is stored in the photo. Everything you do before or after the flash does not matter. A flip-flop is a memory cell that works like that flash. It looks at its input only at one instant, the edge of the clock, and stores that value until the next edge. Last lesson we saw that latches are transparent while enabled, which causes races. Flip-flops fix that problem, and they are the memory cells inside almost every register, counter and processor. In this lesson we learn edge triggering, the master-slave idea, the three main flip-flops D, JK and T, their characteristic and excitation tables, and the timing rules called setup and hold.

Level vs edge triggering: A latch is level sensitive: it responds the whole time the enable is at its active level, which is like a door left open. A flip-flop is edge triggered: it responds only at a clock transition. A positive-edge-triggered flip-flop samples its input when the clock goes from 0 to 1 (the rising edge). A negative-edge-triggered one samples when the clock goes from 1 to 0 (the falling edge). In symbols, a small triangle at the clock input means edge triggered, and a bubble before the triangle means negative edge.

The master-slave D flip-flop: One classic way to build an edge-triggered D flip-flop is to put two D latches in series. The first is the master, the second the slave. The master is enabled when the clock is 0, and the slave is enabled when the clock is 1 (through an inverter). While the clock is 0, the master follows D but the slave is closed, so Q does not change. When the clock rises to 1, the master closes and freezes the value D had at that moment, and the slave opens and copies it to Q. While the clock is 1, D can change freely, but the master is closed, so nothing gets through. The result: Q changes only at the rising edge, to the value of D just before it.

Why this kills the race: Because the master and slave are never open together, there is never a clear path from D to Q. Even if Q feeds back through logic to D, the new D cannot pass until the next rising edge. One edge, one update. This is exactly what counters and state machines need.

The D flip-flop: The D flip-flop is the simplest and most used. Its characteristic equation is Q(t+1) = D. Whatever D is at the clock edge becomes the new Q. Its characteristic table has just two rows: D = 0 gives Q(t+1) = 0, D = 1 gives Q(t+1) = 1. To hold a value, you must feed Q back to D, often through a MUX with a load control. The classic 7474 chip contains two positive-edge-triggered D flip-flops with preset and clear inputs.

The JK flip-flop: The JK flip-flop is like an improved SR flip-flop with no forbidden input. J acts like set and K like reset. J = 0, K = 0: no change. J = 0, K = 1: reset to 0. J = 1, K = 0: set to 1. J = 1, K = 1: toggle, which means Q becomes Q'. Its characteristic equation is Q(t+1) = JQ' + K'Q. Check J = K = 1: Q(t+1) = Q' + 0 = Q', toggle. Check J = K = 0: Q(t+1) = 0 + Q = Q, hold. A JK flip-flop can be built from a D flip-flop with D = JQ' + K'Q.

The race-around problem: In an old level-triggered JK flip-flop with J = K = 1, the output keeps toggling for as long as the clock pulse stays high, because each new Q feeds back and toggles it again. If the pulse is longer than the propagation delay, the final value is unpredictable. This is called the race-around condition. Master-slave and edge-triggered designs solve it, because the output can change only once per clock cycle.

The T flip-flop: T stands for toggle. If T = 0, Q holds. If T = 1, Q toggles at each clock edge. The characteristic equation is Q(t+1) = T ⊕ Q. You can make a T flip-flop from a JK flip-flop by tying J and K together as T, or from a D flip-flop with D = T ⊕ Q. With T = 1 permanently, the output toggles every clock edge, so its frequency is half of the clock's. That is a frequency divider, and chains of T flip-flops form binary counters.

Characteristic tables vs excitation tables: A characteristic table answers "given the inputs and the present state, what is the next state?" It is used for analysis. An excitation table answers the opposite question: "I want to go from Q to Q(t+1); what inputs do I need?" It is used for design, which we do in lesson 21. Every exam on sequential design needs the excitation tables, so learn them well.

D excitation table: The needed D is simply the next state. 0 → 0 needs D = 0. 0 → 1 needs D = 1. 1 → 0 needs D = 0. 1 → 1 needs D = 1. So D = Q(t+1). This is why D flip-flops make design so easy.

JK excitation table: 0 → 0: J = 0, K = X (either hold or reset keeps it 0). 0 → 1: J = 1, K = X (either set or toggle gives 1). 1 → 0: J = X, K = 1 (either reset or toggle gives 0). 1 → 1: J = X, K = 0 (either hold or set keeps 1). The many X entries are don't-cares that make JK designs simpler in K-maps.

T excitation table: T = 1 whenever the state must change, T = 0 when it stays. 0 → 0: T = 0. 0 → 1: T = 1. 1 → 0: T = 1. 1 → 1: T = 0. So T = Q ⊕ Q(t+1). For completeness, the SR flip-flop excitation table is 0 → 0: S = 0, R = X; 0 → 1: S = 1, R = 0; 1 → 0: S = 0, R = 1; 1 → 1: S = X, R = 0.

A worked JK timing example: Take a negative-edge JK flip-flop starting at Q = 0. At falling edge 1, J = 1 and K = 0, so it sets: Q = 1. At edge 2, J = 0 and K = 0, so it holds: Q = 1. At edge 3, J = 1 and K = 1, so it toggles: Q = 0. At edge 4, J = 0 and K = 1, so it resets: Q stays 0. At edge 5, J = 1 and K = 1 again, so it toggles: Q = 1. Notice that between edges, J and K may wiggle as much as they like; only their values at each falling edge count. Practising a few rows like this is the fastest way to stop mixing up the four JK modes.

Direct preset and clear: Many flip-flops also have asynchronous inputs, often called preset (PRE) and clear (CLR), usually active low. They force Q to 1 or 0 immediately, without waiting for a clock edge. They are used to put a system into a known starting state when power comes on, the reset you see in every processor. During normal operation they are kept inactive.

Setup time and hold time: A flip-flop needs D to be stable for a short time before the clock edge, called the setup time tsu, and for a short time after the edge, called the hold time th. If D changes inside that window, the flip-flop may store the wrong value or go into a weird in-between state. The time from the clock edge until Q actually changes is the clock-to-Q delay, tcq. For example, a flip-flop might have tsu = 2 ns, th = 1 ns and tcq = 3 ns.

Maximum clock frequency: In a synchronous circuit, data leaves one flip-flop at a clock edge, passes through combinational logic and must reach the next flip-flop before its setup time. So the clock period must satisfy T ≥ tcq + tcomb + tsu. Example: tcq = 3 ns, logic delay 10 ns, tsu = 2 ns gives T ≥ 15 ns, so the maximum frequency is 1 / 15 ns, about 66.7 MHz. To run faster, you must shorten the logic path or use faster flip-flops. This simple formula connects this lesson with the timing lesson.

Metastability: If setup or hold time is violated, for example when an input comes from a button or another system with a different clock, a flip-flop can become metastable: its output hovers between 0 and 1 for an unpredictable time before falling to one side. Designers reduce the risk by passing such signals through two flip-flops in a row, called a synchronizer, which gives the first one a full clock cycle to settle.

Real life example 1, a digital wall clock: The cheap digital clocks sold in New Market use a 32,768 Hz crystal. That number is 2^15, so a chain of 15 toggling flip-flops, each halving the frequency, turns it into exactly 1 Hz, one tick per second. Each stage is a T flip-flop with T = 1. Further counters made of flip-flops then count seconds, minutes and hours.

Real life example 2, mobile phone processors: Inside your phone's processor, billions of transistors form huge numbers of flip-flops in registers and pipelines. Every clock edge, each flip-flop captures the result of the logic before it. The phone's maximum speed is set by the formula T ≥ tcq + tcomb + tsu for its slowest path. When chip makers advertise a higher clock speed, they have made that sum smaller with faster transistors and shorter logic paths.

Common mistakes: Students confuse characteristic tables with excitation tables, using one when the other is needed. Some write JK excitation without don't-cares, which wastes simplification. Others think a D flip-flop holds its value when D = 0; it does not, it stores 0. Another frequent error is mixing positive- and negative-edge triggering when drawing timing diagrams; always check the symbol. And remember, a T flip-flop with T = 1 divides the clock frequency by 2.

What exams ask: "Distinguish latch and flip-flop", "Explain the master-slave D flip-flop", "Write characteristic tables and equations of D, JK and T flip-flops", "Write the excitation tables", "What is race-around and how is it removed?", "Convert a JK flip-flop into a T (or D) flip-flop", "Define setup and hold time and find the maximum clock frequency", and timing diagrams for given clock and input waveforms.

Recap: Flip-flops are edge triggered: they sample their input only at a clock edge, unlike transparent latches. A master-slave pair of latches gives edge behaviour. D: Q(t+1) = D. JK: Q(t+1) = JQ' + K'Q, with J = K = 1 toggling. T: Q(t+1) = T ⊕ Q. Excitation tables tell which inputs produce a desired change: D = Q(t+1), T = Q ⊕ Q(t+1), and JK uses many don't-cares. Setup time, hold time and clock-to-Q delay set the maximum clock frequency, T ≥ tcq + tcomb + tsu. Next lesson: analysing clocked sequential circuits made of these flip-flops.
key_points: Flip-flops are edge triggered; latches are level sensitive and transparent.
Master-slave: two latches enabled on opposite clock levels give an edge-triggered flip-flop.
D: Q(t+1) = D. JK: Q(t+1) = JQ' + K'Q. T: Q(t+1) = T ⊕ Q.
JK with J = K = 1 toggles; edge triggering removes the race-around problem.
Asynchronous preset and clear force Q immediately, used for power-on reset.
Clock period must satisfy T ≥ tcq + tcomb + tsu; violating setup/hold can cause metastability.
lessons.tip: Write the four JK excitation rows on a small card and keep it while practising design problems. After ten problems you will know them by heart, and they are in almost every sequential design question.
lessons.task: Draw a clock with 6 rising edges and a D input that changes at random times between edges. Draw Q for a positive-edge D flip-flop and for a D latch enabled while the clock is high. Then draw Q for a T flip-flop with T = 1 on the same clock and check that its frequency is half.

quiz.explain: It gives hold (00), reset (01), set (10) and toggle (11).

quiz.q: For a JK flip-flop, which inputs take Q from 1 to 0?
quiz.explain: Either reset (J=0,K=1) or toggle (J=1,K=1) works, so J = X, K = 1.

quiz.q: A T flip-flop with T = 1 fed by a 10 kHz clock produces an output of:
quiz.explain: It toggles once per clock edge, so a full output cycle takes two clock cycles.
