The input needed for a T flip-flop to go from Q = 0 to Q = 1 is:

lessons.title: Analysis of Clocked Sequential Circuits
lessons.content:
Imagine a traffic police officer at Farmgate crossing. What he does next depends on two things: what he sees right now (cars waiting, an ambulance coming) and what he was doing a moment ago (which road he let go last). He has a memory of the situation. A clocked sequential circuit is exactly like that. Its outputs and its next step depend on the present inputs and on what it has stored in its flip-flops. In the last two lessons you met latches and flip-flops, the memory cells. Now we learn to read a whole circuit made of flip-flops and gates, and describe its behaviour with equations, a state table and a state diagram. This skill is called analysis.

What a clocked sequential circuit is: It has two parts. A combinational part made of gates, and a memory part made of flip-flops that all share one clock. The values stored in the flip-flops are called the state. On every clock edge, the flip-flops load new values computed by the gates from the present state and the inputs. Between clock edges, the state stays fixed. So time moves in steps: t, t + 1, t + 2, like the ticks of a clock.

States and flip-flops: With n flip-flops, the circuit can have at most 2^n different states. Two flip-flops A and B give four possible states: 00, 01, 10 and 11. We write the present state as A(t) or just A, and the next state, after the clock edge, as A(t + 1), sometimes written A+.

The analysis procedure in short: Step 1: write the flip-flop input equations, the Boolean expressions feeding each flip-flop input, read from the circuit. Step 2: write the output equations. Step 3: turn the input equations into state equations, which give the next state, using the characteristic equation of the flip-flop type. Step 4: fill the state table. Step 5: draw the state diagram. Step 6: describe in words what the circuit does.

Characteristic equations you need: For a D flip-flop, Q(t + 1) = D. For a T flip-flop, Q(t + 1) = T ⊕ Q, so it toggles when T = 1. For a JK flip-flop, Q(t + 1) = JQ' + K'Q. With D flip-flops, the state equation is the same as the input equation, which makes analysis easy. With JK and T you must substitute.

Worked example with D flip-flops, the equations: A circuit has two D flip-flops A and B, an input x and an output y. Reading the gates gives DA = Ax + Bx, DB = A'x and y = (A + B)x'. Since these are D flip-flops, the state equations are A(t + 1) = Ax + Bx and B(t + 1) = A'x.

Worked example, the state table: List every combination of present state AB and input x, eight rows in total, and compute the next state and the output. Present 00: with x = 0 the next state is 00 and y = 0; with x = 1, A+ = 0 and B+ = 1, so the next state is 01, y = 0. Present 01: with x = 0, next 00 and y = (0 + 1)·1 = 1; with x = 1, A+ = 1 and B+ = 1, next 11, y = 0. Present 10: with x = 0, next 00, y = 1; with x = 1, A+ = 1, B+ = 0, next 10, y = 0. Present 11: with x = 0, next 00, y = 1; with x = 1, next 10, y = 0.

Two layouts of a state table: The first layout has one row per combination of present state and input, as above, with columns for present state, input, next state and output. The second, more compact layout has one row per present state, and separate columns for "next state when x = 0", "next state when x = 1", "output when x = 0" and "output when x = 1". Both carry the same information; use whichever the question shows.

Worked example, reading the behaviour: Look at the table. While x stays 1, the circuit moves 00 → 01 → 11 → 10 → 10 and stays in 10. Whenever x = 0 arrives, it goes back to 00, and the output y is 1 if the circuit was in any state other than 00. So y = 1 means "a 0 has arrived after a run of one or more 1s". In other words, it detects the end of a group of 1s. Analysis lets you discover this meaning from gates alone.

Tracing an input sequence: A good way to check your table is to feed the circuit a sequence of inputs, one per clock, and follow it. Start in 00 and apply x = 1, 1, 0, 1, 0. Clock 1: in 00 with x = 1, output y = 0, move to 01. Clock 2: in 01 with x = 1, y = 0, move to 11. Clock 3: in 11 with x = 0, y = 1, move to 00. Clock 4: in 00 with x = 1, y = 0, move to 01. Clock 5: in 01 with x = 0, y = 1, move to 00. The output sequence is 0, 0, 1, 0, 1. Each 1 appears exactly when a 0 follows some 1s, which confirms our reading. Exams often ask for this kind of trace or a timing diagram.

Reset and the starting state: A real circuit needs a known starting state, otherwise the flip-flops power up with random values. Most designs have a reset input wired to the asynchronous clear of every flip-flop, so pressing reset forces the state to 00. In a state diagram, the reset state is often marked with an extra arrow coming from nowhere. When you analyse a circuit, always say which state it starts in.

The state diagram: A state diagram is a picture of the state table. Each state is a circle with its binary value inside. Each arrow goes from the present state to the next state and is labelled with "input/output". For our example, from 01 there is an arrow to 11 labelled 1/0 and an arrow to 00 labelled 0/1. A state diagram with 4 states and 1 input has exactly 8 arrows, two leaving each state. Diagrams are easier for humans to understand; tables are easier for computing.

Analysis with T flip-flops: Take two T flip-flops A and B, input x and output y, with TA = Bx, TB = x and y = AB. State equations: A(t + 1) = A ⊕ Bx and B(t + 1) = B ⊕ x. When x = 0, nothing toggles, so the state stays the same. When x = 1, B toggles every clock and A toggles when B = 1. Starting at 00: 01, 10, 11, 00, and so on. It is a 2-bit binary counter that counts only when x = 1, and y = 1 when the count is 11.

Analysis with JK flip-flops: Suppose JA = B, KA = Bx', JB = x' and KB = A ⊕ x. Use Q+ = JQ' + K'Q for each. For A: A+ = BA' + (Bx')'A = A'B + AB' + Ax. For B: B+ = x'B' + (A ⊕ x)'B. Then you fill the table exactly as before. A practical shortcut: for each row, find J and K, then apply the JK rule: 00 keep, 01 reset, 10 set, 11 toggle. For example, at A = 0, B = 1, x = 0: JA = 1, KA = 1, so A toggles to 1.

Mealy machines: In our D flip-flop example, the output y = (A + B)x' depends on the input x as well as on the state. Such a circuit is called a Mealy machine. In its state diagram, outputs are written on the arrows as "x/y". A Mealy output can change as soon as the input changes, even in the middle of a clock period. That makes Mealy machines react quickly, but if the input has a glitch, the output may show a brief false value. Designers often register Mealy outputs to avoid this.

Moore machines: In the T flip-flop example, y = AB depends only on the state. Such a circuit is a Moore machine. In its state diagram, the output is written inside the circle, like "11/1", and arrows carry only the input value. Moore outputs change only after a clock edge, so they are steady for a whole clock period. The trade-off is that a Moore machine often needs more states than an equivalent Mealy machine, and its response comes one clock later.

Mealy vs Moore in one table of words: Mealy: output = f(state, input); outputs on arrows; can need fewer states; output may change between clock edges. Moore: output = f(state); outputs inside states; may need extra states; output synchronised with the clock. Any Mealy machine can be converted to an equivalent Moore machine and vice versa, so they are equally powerful.

Real life example 1, a metro rail entry gate: The turnstile at a Dhaka Metro Rail station has two states: locked and unlocked. Input "valid card tapped" moves it from locked to unlocked. Input "person pushes through" moves it from unlocked back to locked. Tapping again while already unlocked keeps it unlocked. If we say the output "green light on" depends only on the state (unlocked), it is a Moore machine. Draw it: two circles, four arrows. That is a real state diagram you walk through every day.

Real life example 2, a washing machine: An automatic washing machine runs through states: fill, wash, rinse, spin, done. The state changes when timers finish or sensors report "water full". The motor and valve outputs depend on the current state, so it is mostly a Moore-style design. Engineers who build the controller first draw this state diagram, then turn it into flip-flops and gates or into a small program on a microcontroller.

Common mistakes: Students forget to use the characteristic equation for JK or T flip-flops and treat the input equation as the next state, which is only true for D. Another mistake is missing rows: with n flip-flops and m inputs, the full table has 2^(n + m) rows. Students also mix the two diagram styles, writing Moore outputs on arrows. For Mealy outputs, remember the output is read for the present state and present input, not the next state.

What exams ask: "Derive the state equations, state table and state diagram for the given circuit", "Is this circuit Mealy or Moore? Why?", "Analyse this circuit with JK flip-flops", "Compare Mealy and Moore machines", and "What does this circuit do?". A neat answer always has: input equations, state equations, a full state table, a diagram, and one sentence describing the function.

Recap: A clocked sequential circuit is gates plus flip-flops sharing a clock; the flip-flop values are the state. Analysis goes input equations, state equations (using the characteristic equation), state table, state diagram, and a description in words. With n flip-flops there are up to 2^n states. Mealy outputs depend on state and input and are written on arrows; Moore outputs depend only on state and are written inside circles. Next lesson we reverse the process and design sequential circuits from a word description.
key_points: Clocked sequential circuit = combinational gates + flip-flops on one clock; flip-flop values are the state.
n flip-flops give at most 2^n states.
Analysis: input equations, state equations, state table, state diagram, description in words.
Characteristic equations: D: Q+ = D; T: Q+ = T ⊕ Q; JK: Q+ = JQ' + K'Q.
State diagram: circles for states, arrows for transitions; Mealy arrows read input/output.
Mealy: output depends on state and input; Moore: output depends on state only.
Moore outputs change only on clock edges; Mealy outputs can change whenever the input changes.
lessons.tip: Before filling any state table, write the present state and input columns in plain binary counting order. Then compute one column at a time (A+, then B+, then y) instead of one row at a time. You make far fewer mistakes.
lessons.task: Analyse a circuit with two D flip-flops where DA = A ⊕ B, DB = B' and output y = AB. Write the state table, draw the state diagram starting from 00, and say in one sentence what the circuit does. Is it Mealy or Moore?

quiz.q: A sequential circuit has 3 flip-flops. At most how many states can it have?
quiz.explain: n flip-flops give at most 2^n states, so 2^3 = 8.

quiz.q: For a T flip-flop, the next state Q(t + 1) is:
quiz.explain: A T flip-flop toggles when T = 1 and holds when T = 0, so Q+ = T ⊕ Q.

quiz.q: In a Moore machine, the output depends on:
quiz.explain: Moore outputs are functions of the present state alone.

quiz.q: With DA = Ax + Bx and DB = A'x, what is the next state from AB = 01 with x = 1?
quiz.explain: A+ = 0·1 + 1·1 = 1 and B+ = 1·1 = 1, so the next state is 11.

quiz.q: In a Mealy state diagram, an arrow labelled 1/0 means:
options: Input 1 gives output 0 on this transition
The clock is 1 and reset is 0
quiz.explain: Mealy arrows are labelled input/output.

lessons.title: Design of Clocked Sequential Circuits
lessons.content:
Think about a bKash PIN check. The app does not care about any single digit by itself. It cares about the sequence: the right digits, in the right order. If you type one wrong digit, it starts watching from the beginning again. A circuit that watches a stream of bits and shouts "found it!" when a pattern appears is called a sequence detector, and it is the classic first design problem for sequential circuits. In the last lesson you analysed circuits, going from gates to a state diagram. Now we go the other way: from a word description to a state diagram, then to flip-flop equations and gates. That is sequential circuit design.

The design procedure: Step 1: understand the word description and draw a state diagram. Step 2: build the state table. Step 3: reduce the number of states if possible. Step 4: give each state a binary code (state assignment). Step 5: choose the flip-flop type (D, JK or T). Step 6: build the excitation table: for each row, what must the flip-flop inputs be to move from the present state to the next state? Step 7: simplify the flip-flop input equations and output equations with K-maps. Step 8: draw the circuit and check it, including unused states.

From words to a state diagram: This is the creative step. Each state should mean something in plain words, like "nothing useful seen yet", "just saw a 1" or "saw 1 then 0". Ask for every state and every input: where do I go now, and what do I output? If you can name each state in a sentence, your diagram is probably right.

Example specification: Design a Mealy circuit with input x and output y. y must be 1 whenever the last three bits received are 1, 0, 1, in that order. Overlapping is allowed, so in the stream 10101 the pattern is found twice: at bit 3 and at bit 5.

Building the states: S0 means "no part of the pattern seen". S1 means "the last bit was 1, the start of the pattern". S2 means "the last two bits were 1, 0". From S0: input 1 goes to S1, input 0 stays in S0, output 0. From S1: input 0 goes to S2; input 1 stays in S1, because the new 1 can be a fresh start; output 0. From S2: input 1 completes 101, so output 1, and we go to S1, because that final 1 can start the next pattern (overlap). Input 0 after 10 gives 100, which contains no useful start, so go back to S0 with output 0.

The Moore version of the same detector: In a Moore machine the output belongs to a state, so we need one extra state, S3, meaning "just saw 101", with output 1. S0, S1 and S2 have output 0. From S2, input 1 now goes to S3 instead of S1. From S3, input 1 goes to S1, because the last bit is a 1, and input 0 goes to S2, because the last two bits are 1, 0, which is the start of the next 101. So the Moore detector has 4 states and still fits in 2 flip-flops, but its output becomes 1 one clock later and stays 1 for a whole clock period.

State reduction, the idea: Sometimes your first diagram has more states than needed. Two states are equivalent if, for every input, they give the same output and go to the same next state, or to equivalent next states. Equivalent states can be merged, which can save flip-flops and gates. The formal methods are the implication table and partitioning, but small problems can be done by inspection.

State reduction example: Suppose a table has four states. a: next a or b for x = 0 or 1, outputs 0, 0. b: next a or c, outputs 0, 0. c: next a or d, outputs 0, 1. d: next a or d, outputs 0, 1. Compare c and d: same outputs (0 for x = 0, 1 for x = 1), same next state for x = 0 (a), and for x = 1 they go to d and d. So c and d are equivalent. Remove d and replace every d with c. Now c goes to c on x = 1. Three states remain: a, b and c, and the circuit is a detector for three 1s in a row. Three states need 2 flip-flops instead of possibly more, and the logic is smaller.

State assignment: Each state gets a binary code. With m states you need at least ⌈log2 m⌉ flip-flops: 3 states need 2, 5 states need 3. Common choices: plain binary (00, 01, 10), Gray code order, where neighbouring states differ by one bit, and one-hot, where each state has its own flip-flop and exactly one flip-flop is 1 at any time. One-hot uses more flip-flops but often gives very simple logic; it is popular in FPGAs, which have many flip-flops. Different assignments give different amounts of logic, and there is no simple rule that always finds the best one.

Our assignment for the 101 detector: Use two flip-flops A and B with S0 = 00, S1 = 01, S2 = 10. The code 11 is unused, so it becomes a don't-care in the K-maps.

The state table with codes: Present AB, input x, next AB, output y. 00, 0 → 00, 0. 00, 1 → 01, 0. 01, 0 → 10, 0. 01, 1 → 01, 0. 10, 0 → 00, 0. 10, 1 → 01, 1. Rows with AB = 11 are don't-cares.

Excitation tables: An excitation table tells you which flip-flop input is needed for each transition Q → Q+. For D: D = Q+, simply. For T: T = 1 when the bit must change, T = 0 when it stays, so T = Q ⊕ Q+. For JK: 0 → 0 needs J = 0, K = X; 0 → 1 needs J = 1, K = X; 1 → 0 needs J = X, K = 1; 1 → 1 needs J = X, K = 0. The many X values in JK tables are why JK designs often simplify nicely.

Design with D flip-flops: DA = A+, which is 1 only for row 01, 0 (minterm 2 of A, B, x), with don't-cares at minterms 6 and 7. The K-map gives DA = Bx'. DB = B+, which is 1 for rows 00,1 and 01,1 and 10,1 (minterms 1, 3, 5) with don't-care 7. That gives DB = x. Output y is 1 only for 10,1 (minterm 5), with don't-cares 6 and 7, so y = Ax. The whole detector is two D flip-flops, one AND with an inverter for DA, one AND for y, and a wire for DB. Beautifully small.

Check it with a sequence: Start at 00 and feed 1, 1, 0, 1. First 1: y = 0, next 01. Second 1: DA = Bx' = 0, DB = 1, next 01, y = 0. Then 0: DA = 1, DB = 0, next 10, y = 0. Then 1: y = Ax = 1. Detected! Next state is 01, ready for overlap.

Design with JK flip-flops: Use the JK excitation table row by row. For A: in rows with A = 0, A+ is 0, 0, 1, 0, so JA = 0, 0, 1, 0 and KA = X. In rows with A = 1, A+ is 0, so KA = 1 and JA = X. K-maps give JA = Bx' and KA = 1. For B: rows with B = 0 need JB equal to the next B, which equals x, and rows with B = 1 need KB = 1 when x = 0 and 0 when x = 1. So JB = x and KB = x'. Same circuit behaviour, different equations.

Design with T flip-flops: T = Q ⊕ Q+. A classic is the 3-bit binary up counter with flip-flops A, B, C (A most significant) and no inputs. C toggles every clock, so TC = 1. B toggles when C = 1, so TB = C. A toggles when B and C are both 1, so TA = BC. This pattern, toggle when all lower bits are 1, is the heart of synchronous counters, which we meet in lesson 23.

Unused states and self-correction: Our detector never uses state 11, but noise or power-up could put it there. With DA = Bx' and DB = x, from 11 with x = 0 the next state is 10, and with x = 1 it is 01. Both are valid states, so the circuit recovers by itself. Always check unused states. A circuit that can get stuck in a loop of unused states is a real bug, called a lock-up.

Real life example 1, a digital door lock: Many new apartments in Gulshan and Bashundhara use keypad door locks. The lock is a sequential machine: each correct digit moves it to the next state, a wrong digit sends it back to the start, and the final correct digit drives the output "unlock". After three wrong attempts, another state may lock the keypad for a minute. Designers draw this state diagram first, exactly as we did, before writing firmware or building logic.

Real life example 2, a traffic light controller: A traffic light at a junction cycles through states like "north-south green", "north-south yellow", "east-west green", "east-west yellow". A timer input says when to move on, and a pedestrian button may add a "walk" state. Each state drives the lamps, so it is a Moore machine. With four states, two flip-flops are enough, or four with one-hot coding for simpler logic.

Common mistakes: The biggest mistake is a wrong state diagram, especially forgetting overlap in sequence detectors. For 101 with overlap, after detecting, go to "saw 1", not to the start. Students also forget the don't-cares from unused codes, mix up the JK excitation rows, or use the characteristic table instead of the excitation table. Another common error is giving a Moore design for a Mealy question; a Moore detector for 101 needs an extra state that holds output 1.

What exams ask: "Design a sequence detector for 101 (or 1101, or 0110), overlapping or non-overlapping, using D or JK flip-flops", "Reduce the given state table", "Design a 3-bit counter using T flip-flops", "Write the excitation tables of D, T and JK flip-flops", and "Check whether the design is self-correcting". Draw the diagram carefully, then the rest is K-map work.

Recap: Sequential design goes from words to state diagram, state table, state reduction, state assignment, excitation table, K-maps and circuit. Equivalent states with the same outputs and equivalent next states can be merged. m states need at least ⌈log2 m⌉ flip-flops; one-hot uses m. Excitation: D = Q+; T = Q ⊕ Q+; JK uses the 0X, 1X, X1, X0 rows. Our 101 Mealy detector reduced to DA = Bx', DB = x, y = Ax. Always check unused states. Next lesson: registers and shift registers.
key_points: Design steps: word spec, state diagram, state table, reduction, assignment, excitation, K-maps, circuit, check.
Two states are equivalent if they give the same outputs and go to equivalent next states for every input.
m states need at least ⌈log2 m⌉ flip-flops; one-hot coding uses one flip-flop per state.
Unused state codes become don't-cares in the K-maps.
Overlapping 101 Mealy detector with S0=00, S1=01, S2=10: DA = Bx', DB = x, y = Ax.
Check unused states so the circuit cannot lock up.
lessons.tip: Before drawing any circle, write each state's meaning in one short sentence, like "just saw 10". If you cannot say what a state means, the diagram is not ready, and every later step will be wrong.
lessons.task: Design a Mealy sequence detector for 11 (overlapping) with one input x and output y. Draw the state diagram, assign codes, and derive the D flip-flop equations. Test it on paper with the stream 0111011 and write the output after each bit.

quiz.q: How many flip-flops are needed at minimum for a machine with 5 states?
quiz.explain: ⌈log2 5⌉ = 3, since 2 flip-flops only give 4 codes.

quiz.q: In the JK excitation table, which inputs move Q from 1 to 0?
quiz.explain: To reset from 1, K must be 1; J does not matter.

quiz.q: For a T flip-flop, the required input T for a transition Q → Q+ is:
quiz.explain: T = 1 when the bit changes, so T = Q ⊕ Q+.

quiz.q: In an overlapping 101 Mealy detector, after detecting 101 the next state should mean:
quiz.explain: The last 1 can be the start of the next 101, so go to the "saw 1" state.

quiz.q: Two states can be merged during state reduction when:
options: They have the same binary code
They have the same outputs and equivalent next states for every input
They are adjacent in the state diagram
quiz.explain: That is the definition of equivalent states.

lessons.title: Registers and Shift Registers
lessons.content:
Imagine a row of four tiffin boxes on a shelf, each holding one thing. You can fill all four at once, or you can push a new box in from one end so that every box slides one place along and the last one falls off the other end. A register is exactly that row of boxes, where each box is a flip-flop holding one bit. A shift register is the version where the bits can slide along, one place per clock tick. Registers are the small, super-fast storage inside every processor, and shift registers are how bits move between serial wires and parallel buses. In this lesson we build both and see where they are used.

What a register is: A register is a group of flip-flops that share a common clock, each storing one bit. An n-bit register has n flip-flops and stores an n-bit word. A 4-bit register built from four D flip-flops with inputs I3 to I0 copies all four inputs into its outputs A3 to A0 on every rising clock edge. Registers usually also have a clear input, often asynchronous and active low, that resets all bits to 0 at once.

The problem with the simple register: If the inputs are connected straight to the D inputs, the register loads new data on every single clock edge. But in a real computer the clock never stops, and we want the register to hold its value until we decide to load. We could stop the clock to that register, which is called clock gating, but gating clocks carelessly causes timing problems. The cleaner solution is a load control input.

Register with parallel load: Put a 2-to-1 multiplexer in front of each D input. A control line called Load selects between the new input Ii and the flip-flop's own output Ai. When Load = 1, Di = Ii, so new data enters at the next clock edge. When Load = 0, Di = Ai, so the flip-flop reloads its own value and nothing changes. In equations: Di = Load·Ii + Load'·Ai. The clock keeps running, and Load decides. Example: A = 0101, inputs I = 1100. Clock with Load = 0: A stays 0101. Clock with Load = 1: A becomes 1100.

Registers inside a processor: A CPU is full of registers. The program counter holds the address of the next instruction. The instruction register holds the instruction being decoded. General-purpose registers, often 16 or 32 of them grouped in a register file, hold the numbers the program is working on right now. In a 64-bit processor each of these is 64 flip-flops wide. Registers are the fastest storage in the whole computer, much faster than cache or main memory, but there are very few of them, which is why compilers work hard to keep the most used variables in registers.

Register transfer notation: Designers describe data movement between registers with a short notation. R2 ← R1 means "copy the contents of R1 into R2 at the next clock edge". A condition can be added in front: T1: R2 ← R1 means the transfer happens only when control signal T1 = 1. In hardware this is exactly a parallel-load register R2 whose inputs come from R1 and whose Load line is T1. Statements like R1 ← R1 + R2 mean an adder sits between the registers. You will use this notation a lot in computer architecture courses.

What a shift register is: A shift register is a chain of flip-flops where each flip-flop's output feeds the next one's input. On each clock edge, every bit moves one position. The first flip-flop takes a new bit from a serial input, and the bit in the last flip-flop leaves through the serial output. A 4-bit shift-right register with D flip-flops is just: D3 = serial in, D2 = A3, D1 = A2, D0 = A1, and serial out = A0.

Shifting step by step: Start a 4-bit shift register at 0000 and feed serial input bits 1, 0, 1, 1, one per clock, shifting right. After clock 1: 1000. After clock 2: 0100. After clock 3: 1010. After clock 4: 1101. The first bit we sent is now in the last flip-flop, ready to come out of the serial output. If we keep clocking with serial input 0, the bits 1, 0, 1, 1 come out of the serial output in the same order they went in, one per clock, and the register slowly empties to 0000. This first-in, first-out behaviour is why a shift register can act as a small queue or a delay line. Draw this as a little table; exams love it.

The four types by input and output: Shift registers are named by how data goes in and comes out. SISO, serial in serial out: bits enter one at a time and leave one at a time; it works as a delay line. In a 4-bit SISO, a bit entering at clock 1 appears at the output after 4 clock edges. SIPO, serial in parallel out: bits enter one at a time, and after n clocks all n bits can be read together; it converts serial to parallel. PISO, parallel in serial out: all bits load at once, then shift out one per clock; it converts parallel to serial. PIPO, parallel in parallel out: load all, read all; this is basically the parallel-load register.

Shifting and arithmetic: For unsigned binary numbers, shifting left by one place multiplies by 2, and shifting right by one place divides by 2, dropping the remainder. 0011 (3) shifted left becomes 0110 (6). 1100 (12) shifted right becomes 0110 (6). For signed 2's complement numbers, an arithmetic right shift copies the sign bit into the empty position, so 1100 (−4) becomes 1110 (−2). Processors use these shifts for fast multiplication and division by powers of two.

Bidirectional and universal shift registers: A bidirectional shift register can shift left or right. A universal shift register can also load in parallel and hold. Each stage has a 4-to-1 multiplexer in front of its D input, controlled by two mode lines S1 and S0. In the common textbook version: S1S0 = 00 means no change (Di = Ai), 01 means shift right, 10 means shift left, and 11 means parallel load (Di = Ii). The classic 74194 chip is a 4-bit bidirectional universal shift register built on this idea.

Universal shift register example: A 4-bit universal register holds 1001. Mode 01 (shift right) with serial-right input 0 gives 0100. Mode 10 (shift left) with serial-left input 1 then gives 1001. Mode 00 keeps 1001. Mode 11 with inputs 0110 loads 0110. One block, four behaviours, chosen by two wires.

Serial transfer between registers: Suppose register A must send its 4 bits to register B using one wire. Connect A's serial output to B's serial input, and also back to A's own serial input. Apply a "shift" control for exactly 4 clock pulses. Each clock, one bit leaves A and enters B, and the same bit re-enters A. After 4 clocks, B holds A's old value, and A still holds its value because it rotated all the way around. Serial transfer uses one wire but takes n clocks; parallel transfer uses n wires but needs one clock. That is the classic trade-off.

The serial adder: A neat circuit combines two shift registers, one full adder and one D flip-flop. Registers A and B shift out their bits, least significant first. The full adder adds the two bits and the stored carry. The sum bit is shifted back into register A, and the carry-out is stored in the D flip-flop for the next clock. After n clocks, A holds the sum. It uses only one full adder instead of n, so it is small, but slow. This shows how sequential circuits can trade time for hardware.

Real chips you will meet: The 74HC595 is a popular SIPO shift register with an output latch. Hobbyists in Bangladesh often use it with an Arduino to control 8 LEDs using only 3 pins: data, clock and latch. Several 595s can be chained for many more LEDs. The 74HC165 is a PISO register used to read 8 buttons into a microcontroller through one data pin. These chips are cheap and easy to find in electronics markets like Patuatuli in Old Dhaka.

Real life example 1, serial communication: When a microcontroller sends data to a GPS module, a Bluetooth module or a computer through a UART port, the transmitter loads a byte in parallel and shifts it out bit by bit (PISO). The receiver shifts the bits in one at a time and then reads the whole byte (SIPO). USB, SATA and PCIe are also serial links today, because sending bits one after another very fast over a few wires turned out to be easier than keeping dozens of parallel wires perfectly in step.

Real life example 2, a scrolling LED sign: Shops in Bangladesh often have a red LED board scrolling "Welcome" or the day's offers. Behind it, rows of LEDs are fed by shift registers. The controller shifts in new columns of pixels, each shift moves the picture one step, and the message seems to slide across the board. It is exactly the "tiffin boxes sliding along the shelf" picture from the start of this lesson.

Common mistakes: Students forget the Load = 0 path that feeds a flip-flop's output back to itself, and then the register cannot hold. In shift tables, students shift in the wrong direction or forget that the new bit enters at the serial input end. Another frequent mistake is the clock count: in an n-bit SISO, a bit needs n clock edges to reach the output. Do not confuse logical right shift (fill with 0) with arithmetic right shift (copy the sign bit). Finally, gating the clock with an AND gate is shown in some books, but in real designs it can cause glitches and timing skew, so a load-enable multiplexer is preferred.

What exams ask: "Design a 4-bit register with parallel load", "Draw a 4-bit shift register and show its contents after each clock for a given serial input", "Explain SISO, SIPO, PISO and PIPO with diagrams", "Design a 4-bit universal shift register using 4-to-1 multiplexers and give its mode table", "Explain serial transfer from register A to B", "Draw a serial adder". Neat timing tables score well.

Recap: A register is n flip-flops with a shared clock storing an n-bit word. A parallel-load register uses a 2-to-1 multiplexer per bit: Di = Load·Ii + Load'·Ai. A shift register passes each bit to the next flip-flop on every clock. SISO, SIPO, PISO and PIPO describe how data enters and leaves. Shifting left multiplies by 2 and right divides by 2 for unsigned numbers. A universal shift register uses 4-to-1 multiplexers with mode bits for hold, right, left and load. Serial transfer uses one wire and n clocks. Next lesson: counters, which are registers that step through a sequence of states.
key_points: A register is a group of flip-flops on a common clock; an n-bit register stores an n-bit word.
Parallel load: a 2-to-1 MUX per bit, Di = Load·Ii + Load'·Ai, so the register holds when Load = 0.
A shift register moves every bit one position per clock, taking a new bit at the serial input.
SISO, SIPO, PISO, PIPO name how data enters and leaves; SIPO and PISO convert between serial and parallel.
Unsigned shift left multiplies by 2, shift right divides by 2; arithmetic right shift keeps the sign bit.
Universal shift register: a 4-to-1 MUX per stage; S1S0 = 00 hold, 01 right, 10 left, 11 load.
Serial transfer uses one wire and n clocks; parallel transfer uses n wires and one clock.
lessons.tip: For every shift register question, draw a table with one row per clock and one column per flip-flop, and fill it row by row. Write the new serial bit at the input end first, then copy the old bits one step along.
lessons.task: Draw a 4-bit shift-right register starting at 0000. Feed serial input bits 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0 and write the contents after each clock. Then load 1011 into a universal shift register and write its contents after modes 01 (serial in 0), 10 (serial in 1) and 00.

quiz.q: In a register with parallel load, what happens on a clock edge when Load = 0?
quiz.explain: With Load = 0, each D input gets the flip-flop's own output, so nothing changes.

quiz.q: Which shift register type converts serial data into parallel data?
quiz.explain: Serial in, parallel out: bits enter one by one and are read together.

quiz.q: Unsigned 0101 shifted left by one place gives:
quiz.explain: Shift left multiplies by 2: 5 becomes 10, which is 1010.

quiz.q: In the textbook universal shift register, mode S1S0 = 11 means:
quiz.explain: 00 hold, 01 shift right, 10 shift left, 11 parallel load.

quiz.q: A 4-bit shift-right register starts at 0000. After serial inputs 1 then 1, its contents are:
quiz.explain: After clock 1: 1000. After clock 2: 1100.

lessons.title: Counters: Ripple, Synchronous, Mod-N, Ring and Johnson
lessons.content:
Think of the token machine at a bank branch in Motijheel. Every time a new customer presses the button, the number goes up by one: 41, 42, 43. When it reaches the end of its range, it starts again. Or think of a cricket scoreboard ticking up run by run. A digital counter does exactly this job. It is a sequential circuit that moves through a fixed sequence of states, one step for each clock pulse. Counters count events, measure time, divide frequencies and step machines through their jobs. In this lesson we build ripple counters, synchronous counters, up/down counters, mod-N and BCD counters, and two special shift-register counters: the ring counter and the Johnson counter.

What a counter is: A counter is a register that goes through a prescribed sequence of states when input pulses arrive. The pulses can be a clock or random events like a person passing a sensor. With n flip-flops, a counter can have at most 2^n states. A counter with N states is called a mod-N counter. A 4-bit binary counter counts 0000 to 1111, which is 0 to 15, so it is mod-16.

The toggle idea: Look at binary counting: 0000, 0001, 0010, 0011, 0100. The lowest bit flips on every count. Bit 1 flips whenever bit 0 goes from 1 to 0. Bit 2 flips whenever bit 1 goes from 1 to 0, and so on. So each bit simply toggles at the right moment. That is why T flip-flops, or JK flip-flops with J = K = 1, are perfect for counters. A T flip-flop with T = 1 complements its output on every active clock edge.

Ripple (asynchronous) counter: In a ripple counter, only the first flip-flop gets the external clock. Each later flip-flop is clocked by the output of the one before it. Use four negative-edge-triggered T flip-flops with T = 1. Q0 toggles on every falling clock edge. Q0 feeds the clock of flip-flop 1, so Q1 toggles whenever Q0 falls from 1 to 0. Q1 clocks flip-flop 2, and Q2 clocks flip-flop 3. The result counts up 0, 1, 2 ... 15 and back to 0. If you use positive-edge flip-flops instead, connect each clock to the previous Q' to keep counting up, or to Q to count down.

Why it is called ripple: The flip-flops do not change together. When the count goes from 0111 to 1000, Q0 changes first, then its fall makes Q1 change, then Q2, then Q3. Each step adds one flip-flop delay. For a short moment the outputs pass through wrong values: 0111 becomes 0110, then 0100, then 0000, and finally 1000. These short false states can cause glitches if another circuit decodes the outputs. Also, the total delay grows with the number of bits, so the maximum clock speed drops for long ripple counters.

Ripple counter strengths: Ripple counters are very simple and use little power and hardware, so they are still used for slow jobs like dividing a clock in a cheap wall clock. The classic 7493 chip is a 4-bit ripple binary counter, and the 7490 is a ripple decade counter.

Synchronous counter: In a synchronous counter, every flip-flop receives the same clock, so all bits change together. Gates decide which flip-flops should toggle. Rule for counting up: a bit toggles when all lower bits are 1. With T flip-flops: T0 = 1, T1 = Q0, T2 = Q0Q1, T3 = Q0Q1Q2. Check from 0111: T0 = 1, T1 = 1, T2 = 1, T3 = 1, so all four bits flip at the same edge, giving 1000 directly with no false states in between. Check from 0101: T1 = 1, T2 = Q0Q1 = 0, T3 = 0, so only bits 0 and 1 flip, giving 0110. Correct.

Count enable and chaining: Real synchronous counters have a count enable input. Then T0 = EN, T1 = EN·Q0, and so on. The AND chain also produces a carry output when all bits are 1 and EN = 1, which can enable the next 4-bit counter. This lets you build 8-bit or 16-bit counters that still change on one common clock. The 74161 is a well-known synchronous 4-bit binary counter with parallel load, count enables and a carry output.

Down counter and up/down counter: To count down, a bit toggles when all lower bits are 0: T1 = Q0', T2 = Q0'Q1', T3 = Q0'Q1'Q2'. From 1000, every lower bit is 0, so all bits flip and the next state is 0111. To make one counter do both, add a control input. With Up and Down signals: T1 = Up·Q0 + Down·Q0', T2 = Up·Q0Q1 + Down·Q0'Q1', and so on. When Up = 1 the counter counts up; when Down = 1 it counts down.

Designing any counter from a state table: A counter is just a sequential circuit with no external inputs except the clock, so you can design it with the method from the sequential design lesson. Write the present state and next state, use the flip-flop excitation table to get the needed T, D or JK inputs, simplify with K-maps, and draw the circuit. Unused states become don't-cares, but you should check that the counter does not get stuck in them after power-up.

Mod-N counters: Sometimes you need a sequence that is not a power of 2, like mod-6 for a dice game or mod-10 for a decimal digit. You need n flip-flops with 2^n ≥ N. For mod-6 you need 3 flip-flops (8 states), and two states are unused. The clean way is synchronous design from a state table with the unused states as don't-cares. A quick and dirty way with a ripple counter is to detect the state N and force an asynchronous clear. For mod-10, a NAND gate on Q3 and Q1 clears the counter when it reaches 1010. The problem is that 1010 appears for a tiny moment, a glitch, so this trick is avoided in careful designs.

Mod-N with a parallel-load counter: A cleaner trick uses a counter with synchronous parallel load, like the 74161. Set the data inputs to 0000 and connect a gate that detects the last wanted state to the LOAD input. For mod-6, detect 0101 (count 5) with an AND of Q2 and Q0. While the count is 5, LOAD is active, so at the next clock edge the counter loads 0000 instead of going to 0110. The sequence is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 0, with no glitch state, because the load happens on the clock edge like every other change. The 74161's clear input is asynchronous, so using clear instead would require detecting 6 and would show that short false state again.

BCD (decade) counter: A BCD counter counts 0000 to 1001 and then returns to 0000, so it is mod-10. A synchronous BCD counter with T flip-flops, outputs Q8 Q4 Q2 Q1, has these inputs: T1 = 1, T2 = Q8'Q1, T4 = Q2Q1, T8 = Q8Q1 + Q4Q2Q1. Check the jump from 1001 (9): T1 = 1, T2 = 0, T4 = 0, T8 = 1, so Q1 and Q8 flip and the state becomes 0000. Check 0111 (7): T2 = 1, T4 = 1, T8 = 1, so all bits flip and the state becomes 1000 (8). A carry output, 1 when the count is 9, lets you cascade decade counters for units, tens and hundreds, like a car odometer.

Ring counter: A ring counter is a shift register whose last output feeds back to its first input. Start it with a single 1, like 1000. Each clock shifts the 1 along: 1000, 0100, 0010, 0001, then back to 1000. With n flip-flops it has only n states, which wastes states, but each state is decoded without any gates: the flip-flop that holds the 1 tells you the state directly. Ring counters are used to create timing signals T0, T1, T2, T3 that turn on one after another in a control unit.

Johnson (twisted ring) counter: A Johnson counter feeds the complement of the last output back to the first input. Start at 0000 with 4 flip-flops: 0000, 1000, 1100, 1110, 1111, 0111, 0011, 0001, then back to 0000. That is 2n = 8 states with 4 flip-flops, twice as many as a ring counter. Each state can be decoded with a single 2-input AND gate looking at two neighbouring bits. Both ring and Johnson counters have unused states, so practical designs add logic to correct them if noise or power-up puts the counter into a bad state.

Counters as frequency dividers: Each toggle flip-flop halves the frequency of its clock. So Q0 runs at f/2, Q1 at f/4, Q2 at f/8. A mod-N counter divides by N. A quartz wrist watch uses a crystal at 32,768 Hz, which is 2^15 Hz. A chain of 15 divide-by-2 stages gives exactly 1 Hz, one tick per second. That is why that strange number is chosen.

Real life example 1, the bank token machine: When a customer presses the button at a bank or a passport office in Agargaon, a counter increments and the number is printed. The counter holds its value between presses, unlike a combinational circuit. The display shows the count through BCD counters feeding 7-segment decoders: one decade counter for units, its carry enabling the tens counter, and so on. When the count reaches 999, the next press rolls everything to 000.

Real life example 2, a traffic signal controller: A simple traffic light at a crossing in Chattogram cycles red, green, yellow on fixed timing. A clock of, say, 1 Hz drives a counter that counts seconds. When it reaches certain values, decoders change the lights, and at the end the counter resets. A ring counter is a natural fit for the "one phase at a time" pattern, while a mod-N timer counts the seconds inside each phase.

Common mistakes: Students mix up which edge and which output (Q or Q') to connect in ripple counters, and end up with a down counter. Another mistake is forgetting that ripple counters pass through false intermediate states. In synchronous counters, students write T2 = Q1 instead of T2 = Q0Q1. Students also count the states of a Johnson counter wrong: it is 2n, not 2^n and not n. Finally, in mod-N design, always check the unused states.

What exams ask: "Design a 4-bit synchronous binary up counter with T or JK flip-flops", "Draw a 3-bit ripple counter and its timing diagram", "Design a mod-6 synchronous counter with D flip-flops", "Design a synchronous BCD counter", "Compare ripple and synchronous counters", "Draw the state sequence of a 4-bit Johnson counter and give the decoding gates", "How many flip-flops are needed for a mod-25 counter?" (answer: 5, since 2^5 = 32 ≥ 25).

Recap: Counters are sequential circuits that step through a fixed sequence. Ripple counters chain flip-flop outputs into the next clock; they are simple but slow and glitchy. Synchronous counters share one clock and use T0 = 1, T1 = Q0, T2 = Q0Q1 and so on. Up/down control, count enable and carry outputs make counters flexible. Mod-N and BCD counters stop short of 2^n states. Ring counters have n states, Johnson counters 2n. Every flip-flop stage divides the frequency by two. Next lesson: memory and programmable logic.
key_points: A counter with n flip-flops has at most 2^n states; N states make a mod-N counter.
Ripple counter: each flip-flop is clocked by the previous output; simple but delays add up and false states appear.
Synchronous up counter with T flip-flops: T0 = 1, T1 = Q0, T2 = Q0Q1, T3 = Q0Q1Q2.
Down counting uses complemented lower bits; an Up/Down control selects between the two.
BCD counter counts 0 to 9; its carry at 9 lets decade counters cascade.
Ring counter has n states with one circulating 1; Johnson counter has 2n states using Q' feedback.
Each toggle stage divides frequency by 2; 32,768 Hz through 15 stages gives 1 Hz.
lessons.tip: Write the binary count from 0000 to 1111 in a column and circle each place where a bit flips. You will see the rule "a bit flips when all bits below it are 1" with your own eyes, and the synchronous counter equations will never be forgotten.
lessons.task: On paper, draw the timing diagram of a 3-bit ripple up counter for 10 clock pulses. Then write the full state sequence of a 3-bit Johnson counter starting from 000 and design the 2-input AND gate that detects each state.

quiz.q: How many states does a 4-bit Johnson counter have?
quiz.explain: A Johnson counter has 2n states, so 2 × 4 = 8.

quiz.q: In a synchronous up counter with T flip-flops, T2 equals:
quiz.explain: A bit toggles when all lower bits are 1, so T2 = Q0Q1.

quiz.q: Which is a disadvantage of a ripple counter?
options: Delays add up and outputs pass through false states
It needs a separate clock for every flip-flop from outside
It needs more gates than a synchronous counter
quiz.explain: Each flip-flop waits for the previous one, so changes ripple and temporary wrong states appear.

quiz.q: Minimum number of flip-flops for a mod-25 counter:
quiz.explain: 2^4 = 16 is too small; 2^5 = 32 ≥ 25, so 5 flip-flops.

quiz.q: A synchronous BCD counter in state 1001 goes next to:
quiz.explain: A BCD counter is mod-10, so after 9 it returns to 0.

lessons.title: Memory, Programmable Logic and Logic Families
lessons.content:
Imagine a huge apartment building in Uttara with thousands of flats, each with a number on the door and a letterbox inside. If you know the flat number, you can drop a letter in or take one out. Computer memory is that building. Each "flat" is a word of bits, the flat number is the address, and reading or writing is like using the letterbox. In this lesson we see how RAM and ROM are organised, how a ROM can act as a logic circuit, how programmable chips like PLA, PAL, CPLD and FPGA let you build hardware without a factory, and finally how real gates differ: TTL and CMOS families, fan-out and noise margin.

Memory words and addresses: A memory unit stores binary information in groups called words. A word might be 8 bits (a byte), 16, 32 or 64 bits. Each word has an address. A memory with k address lines can have 2^k words. If each word is n bits, we call it a 2^k × n memory. Example: a 1K × 8 memory has 1024 words of 8 bits each. It needs 10 address lines, because 2^10 = 1024, and 8 data lines. A 64K × 16 memory needs 16 address lines and 16 data lines.

RAM: RAM stands for random access memory, which means any word can be read or written in about the same time, no matter its address. A RAM chip has address inputs, data inputs and outputs, a read/write control, and a chip select or enable. To write: put the address on the address lines, put the data on the data lines, and activate write. To read: put the address, activate read, and the word appears on the data outputs. Chip select lets many RAM chips share the same buses, with a decoder choosing which chip answers, as you saw in the decoder lesson.

Static vs dynamic RAM: In static RAM (SRAM), each bit is stored in a latch, typically built from 6 transistors. It keeps its value as long as power is on, and it is fast, so it is used for processor cache. In dynamic RAM (DRAM), each bit is stored as charge on a tiny capacitor with one transistor. It is much denser and cheaper per bit, but the charge leaks away, so every cell must be refreshed periodically, typically within tens of milliseconds. The main memory of your laptop is DRAM. Both SRAM and DRAM are volatile: they lose their data when power goes off.

Inside a RAM: decoding the address: A memory needs to pick one word out of 2^k. A single k-to-2^k decoder works but becomes huge. For 1K words, it needs 1024 AND gates with 10 inputs each. The smarter way is two-dimensional, or coincident, decoding: arrange the cells in a square, use 5 address bits for a row decoder (32 rows) and 5 bits for a column decoder (32 columns). A cell is selected where its row and column meet. That uses two 5-to-32 decoders, 64 gates in total, instead of 1024.

ROM: ROM stands for read-only memory. Its contents are fixed and kept even without power, so it is non-volatile. A 2^k × n ROM has k address inputs and n outputs. Inside, a k-to-2^k decoder generates every minterm, and a programmable OR array connects each minterm to the outputs that should be 1. So a ROM is literally a truth table stored in hardware.

Types of ROM: Mask ROM is programmed at the factory with a final mask, cheap only in large quantities. PROM (programmable ROM) has fuses that the user blows once with a programmer; it cannot be changed afterwards. EPROM can be erased with ultraviolet light through a little quartz window and reprogrammed. EEPROM can be erased and reprogrammed electrically, byte by byte. Flash memory is a kind of EEPROM erased in blocks, and it is what your phone storage, pen drives and SSDs use.

ROM as combinational logic: Since a ROM stores a truth table, any combinational circuit with k inputs and n outputs can be built from a 2^k × n ROM. Example: a circuit that takes a 3-bit number and outputs its square. Inputs 0 to 7, squares 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, so the output needs 6 bits. Notice two tricks: bit 0 of the square always equals bit 0 of the input (odd numbers have odd squares), and bit 1 of the square is always 0 (every square divided by 4 leaves 0 or 1). So only 4 outputs need the ROM, and an 8 × 4 ROM is enough. Simple and no K-maps needed.

PLA: A ROM generates every minterm, even ones you never use. A PLA (programmable logic array) is more efficient: it has a programmable AND array that makes only the product terms you need, followed by a programmable OR array that combines them into outputs. Often each output can also be complemented by a programmable XOR. A PLA size is described by inputs, product terms and outputs. Example: F1 = AB' + AC + A'BC' and F2 = (AC + BC)' can share the product term AC. Designers simplify all outputs together to share as many product terms as possible, because the number of product terms is the limited resource.

PAL: A PAL (programmable array logic) has a programmable AND array but a fixed OR array. Each output OR gate gets a fixed number of product terms, for example 4 or 8. A PAL is easier and cheaper to make than a PLA, but product terms cannot be shared between outputs, and if a function needs more terms than one OR gate has, you must feed one output back into the array and use it as an input. In short: PROM has fixed AND and programmable OR; PAL has programmable AND and fixed OR; PLA has both programmable.

CPLD and FPGA: As designs grew, chips grew. A CPLD (complex programmable logic device) puts many PAL-like blocks with flip-flops on one chip, connected by a programmable switch matrix. An FPGA (field programmable gate array) is different inside: it has thousands to millions of small logic blocks, each built around a lookup table (LUT), a tiny memory that can implement any function of its 4 to 6 inputs, plus a flip-flop. Programmable routing connects these blocks, and modern FPGAs add block RAM, multipliers and even processor cores. Most FPGAs store their configuration in SRAM, so they load it from flash at power-up. Engineers use FPGAs to prototype chips, in telecom equipment, in cameras, and anywhere custom high-speed logic is needed in small quantities.

Logic families: what they are: So far gates were perfect symbols. Real gates are built from transistors in a particular style called a logic family. The two most important families are TTL and CMOS. Families differ in supply voltage, speed, power use, how many inputs one output can drive, and how much noise they can tolerate.

TTL: TTL (transistor-transistor logic) uses bipolar junction transistors. The classic 74 series runs on 5 V. Many chips you met in this course, like the 7400 NAND, 7447 decoder or 7493 counter, began life as TTL. Standard TTL guarantees an output high of at least 2.4 V and an output low of at most 0.4 V, and its inputs accept at least 2.0 V as high and at most 0.8 V as low. TTL uses noticeable power even when it is not switching.

CMOS: CMOS (complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor) uses pairs of n-type and p-type MOS transistors. In a steady state, one of the pair is off, so almost no current flows and static power is tiny. Power is mainly used when switching, and it grows with the switching frequency, the load capacitance and the square of the supply voltage. That is why CMOS took over the world: phone processors, laptops and almost every modern chip are CMOS. Families like 74HC copy TTL pin-outs in CMOS.

Fan-out: Fan-out is the number of standard gate inputs that one gate output can drive while still keeping correct voltage levels. A standard TTL output can drive 10 standard TTL inputs, so its fan-out is 10. If you connect too many inputs, the output voltage moves out of the safe range and logic levels become unreliable. CMOS inputs draw almost no steady current, so the static fan-out is large, but each extra input adds capacitance and slows the switching.

Noise margin: Wires pick up electrical noise. Noise margin tells how much noise a signal can carry and still be read correctly. High-level noise margin NMH = VOH(min) − VIH(min). Low-level noise margin NML = VIL(max) − VOL(max). For standard TTL, NMH = 2.4 − 2.0 = 0.4 V and NML = 0.8 − 0.4 = 0.4 V. So a noise spike under 0.4 V cannot flip a TTL logic level. Bigger noise margin means a more robust circuit.

Other parameters: Propagation delay is the time from an input change to the output change, often a few nanoseconds for TTL and much less inside modern CMOS chips. Power dissipation is the power used per gate. The speed-power product, delay times power, is a figure of merit: smaller is better. Exam questions often ask you to compare families on these four numbers: fan-out, noise margin, propagation delay and power.

Real life example 1, your phone storage and memory: A typical phone has some gigabytes of DRAM as working memory and much more flash as storage. When you open the bKash app, its code is copied from flash, which keeps data without power, into DRAM, which is fast but forgets everything when the phone shuts down. Inside the processor, small SRAM caches keep the most used data even closer. All three are memory arrays with addresses and decoders, exactly as in this lesson.

Real life example 2, FPGA in a university lab: Many university labs in Bangladesh use small FPGA boards for digital design courses. Students write a design, the software turns it into LUT contents and routing, and the board becomes a counter, a traffic light controller or even a simple processor in seconds. If the design has a bug, they fix it and reload, with no new chip needed. The same idea lets companies update hardware in base stations and network equipment after it is installed.

Common mistakes: Students mix up address lines and data lines; remember 2^k words need k address lines, and word width decides data lines. Another mistake is saying a PAL has a programmable OR array; it is the AND array that is programmable. Some forget that DRAM needs refresh while SRAM does not. For noise margin, students subtract the wrong pair; always compare an output guarantee with the matching input requirement: VOH with VIH, and VIL with VOL.

What exams ask: "How many address and data lines does a 4K × 16 memory need?" (12 and 16), "Implement this function using a ROM and give its truth table", "Implement two functions with a PLA and show the programming table", "Compare PROM, PAL and PLA", "Distinguish SRAM and DRAM", "Calculate the noise margins from given voltage levels", "Define fan-out and propagation delay", "Why is CMOS low power?".

Recap: Memory is an array of 2^k words of n bits, chosen by k address lines through decoders; SRAM uses latches, DRAM uses capacitors that need refresh, and both are volatile. ROM is non-volatile and is a stored truth table, so it can build any combinational function. PLA has programmable AND and OR, PAL programmable AND and fixed OR, and FPGAs use LUTs and flip-flops with programmable routing. TTL and CMOS are logic families compared by fan-out, noise margin, delay and power. The last lesson brings it together with HDL and ASM charts.
key_points: A 2^k × n memory has k address lines and n data lines; 1K × 8 needs 10 address lines.
SRAM stores bits in latches (fast, used for cache); DRAM uses capacitors that need refresh; both are volatile.
ROM is non-volatile: a decoder making all minterms plus a programmable OR array, so it stores a truth table.
ROM types: mask ROM, PROM (one-time fuses), EPROM (UV erase), EEPROM and flash (electrical erase).
PROM: fixed AND, programmable OR; PAL: programmable AND, fixed OR; PLA: both programmable.
FPGA: many LUT-plus-flip-flop blocks with programmable routing, usually configured from SRAM.
Noise margin: NMH = VOH − VIH, NML = VIL − VOL (0.4 V for standard TTL); TTL fan-out is 10; CMOS has tiny static power.
lessons.tip: Make a three-row table on one page: PROM, PAL, PLA, with columns "AND array" and "OR array", and write fixed or programmable in each cell. Half the programmable-logic questions in exams are answered by that single table.
lessons.task: Design a ROM that converts a 3-bit binary input to its 3-bit Gray code. Write the ROM size, its full truth table (address in, data out), and then mark which output bits could be made with a single XOR gate instead.

quiz.q: How many address lines does a 4K × 16 memory need?
quiz.explain: 4K = 4096 = 2^12 words, so 12 address lines; 16 is the data width.

quiz.q: Which memory type must be refreshed periodically?
quiz.explain: DRAM stores bits as charge on capacitors, which leaks away.

quiz.q: A PAL has:
options: Fixed AND array and programmable OR array
Programmable AND array and fixed OR array
quiz.explain: PAL programs the AND array; the OR gates are fixed.

quiz.q: If VOH = 2.4 V and VIH = 2.0 V, the high-level noise margin is:
quiz.explain: NMH = VOH − VIH = 2.4 − 2.0 = 0.4 V.

quiz.q: The basic logic element inside most FPGA blocks is:
options: A lookup table (LUT) with a flip-flop
quiz.explain: Each FPGA logic block uses a small LUT that can implement any function of its inputs, plus a flip-flop.

lessons.title: HDL and ASM Charts: Verilog, Design Flow and Course Recap
lessons.content:
Imagine building a whole housing project in Purbachal by drawing every single brick by hand. Impossible. Architects instead write plans and specifications, and machines and teams turn them into buildings. Digital design went through the same change. In the 1970s, engineers drew gates on paper. A modern phone chip has billions of transistors, so nobody draws them. Designers describe hardware in text using a hardware description language (HDL), and software tools turn that text into gates. In this final lesson we learn Verilog basics, the ASM chart for planning sequential machines, the complete digital design flow, and then we look back at the whole course.

What an HDL is: An HDL looks a bit like a programming language, but it describes hardware, not a list of steps for a CPU. The two famous HDLs are Verilog and VHDL, both IEEE standards. A key difference from normal programming: in hardware, everything runs at the same time. Ten gates on a chip all work in parallel, so many HDL statements are concurrent. An HDL description is used for two jobs: simulation, to test the design on a computer, and synthesis, to turn it into real gates for an FPGA or a chip.

Verilog module: The basic building block in Verilog is a module, like a chip with pins. A half adder looks like this: module half_adder(input a, input b, output s, output c); assign s = a ^ b; assign c = a & b; endmodule. The module has a name, a port list with inputs and outputs, a body, and ends with endmodule. The operators are like C: & for AND, | for OR, ~ for NOT, ^ for XOR.

Continuous assignment with assign: The assign statement describes combinational logic. It means "this wire is always equal to this expression". Whenever a or b changes, s and c update automatically, just like real gates. Order of assign statements does not matter, because they all run concurrently. A full adder can be written as: assign s = a ^ b ^ cin; assign cout = (a & b) | (cin & (a ^ b)); or even more simply as assign {cout, s} = a + b + cin; where the braces join cout and s into a 2-bit result.

Wires, regs and vectors: A wire is a connection, driven by assign or by a module output. A reg is a variable assigned inside an always block; despite the name, it does not always become a register. Vectors carry many bits: wire [3:0] a; declares a 4-bit bus with a[3] as the most significant bit. A 4-bit adder becomes one line: assign {cout, sum} = a + b + cin; where a, b and sum are 4 bits wide.

Structural description: You can also build a design by connecting smaller modules, like placing chips on a board. For a full adder made from two half adders: half_adder ha1(.a(x), .b(y), .s(p), .c(g)); half_adder ha2(.a(p), .b(cin), .s(sum), .c(t)); assign cout = g | t; Each line creates an instance and connects its ports to wires. This style matches the block diagrams you drew in the adder lesson.

Always blocks for combinational logic: An always block runs its body whenever something in its sensitivity list changes. For combinational logic we write always @(*) so that every input is included. A 4-to-1 multiplexer: always @(*) case (sel) 2'b00: y = d0; 2'b01: y = d1; 2'b10: y = d2; default: y = d3; endcase. Here 2'b01 means a 2-bit binary constant 01. Every output must be assigned in every path, or the tool may infer an unwanted latch.

Always blocks for sequential logic: Flip-flops react to clock edges, so we write always @(posedge clk). A D flip-flop is: always @(posedge clk) q <= d; A 4-bit counter with synchronous reset is: always @(posedge clk) if (reset) count <= 4'b0000; else count <= count + 1; That one line replaces the T flip-flop equations from the counter lesson, and the synthesis tool builds the gates for you.

Blocking vs nonblocking: Verilog has two assignment kinds. Blocking (=) happens immediately, in order, like normal code. Nonblocking (<=) evaluates all right-hand sides first and updates all left-hand sides together at the end, which is exactly how flip-flops sharing a clock behave. The rule of thumb: use = in combinational always @(*) blocks and <= in clocked always @(posedge clk) blocks. Example: a shift register always @(posedge clk) begin q1 <= d; q2 <= q1; q3 <= q2; end shifts correctly, because each flip-flop takes the old value of its neighbour. With = it would copy d into all three at once.

Testbenches and simulation: A testbench is a Verilog module with no ports that creates inputs, applies them to the design, and checks the outputs. It uses things like initial blocks and delays, for example #10 a = 1; which are for simulation only and do not become hardware. The simulator shows waveforms that look like the timing diagrams you drew by hand. Testing all rows of a truth table in a testbench takes seconds.

ASM charts: idea: Before writing HDL for a sequential machine, designers often draw an algorithmic state machine (ASM) chart. It looks like a flowchart, but it has a precise timing meaning: it describes a state machine clock cycle by clock cycle. It is especially useful for designs that have a datapath (registers, adders, counters) and a control unit that tells the datapath what to do.

ASM chart symbols: There are three boxes. The state box is a rectangle with the state name and the Moore outputs or register operations done in that state, like "count <- count + 1". The decision box is a diamond that tests an input or status condition and has two exits, 1 and 0. The conditional output box is a box with rounded ends, placed after a decision box; its outputs happen only in that state when that condition is true, which is a Mealy-type output.

ASM block and timing: An ASM block is one state box together with all the decision and conditional boxes that follow it until the next state boxes. One ASM block represents exactly one clock cycle. All the operations in a block happen at the same clock edge at the end of the cycle, and the path chosen through the decision boxes decides the next state. This is very different from a software flowchart, where each box is a separate step in time.

ASM chart example: Design a controller that waits for a Start button, then counts to 3 and signals Done. State S_idle: output Ready = 1; decision Start? If 0, stay in S_idle; if 1, go to S_count with a conditional box "clear counter". State S_count: register operation "count <- count + 1"; decision "count = 2?" If 0, stay; if 1, go to S_done. State S_done: output Done = 1; go back to S_idle. From this chart you can write a state table and design it with flip-flops, or write Verilog directly with a case statement on the state register.

From ASM to Verilog: Code the state as a register: reg [1:0] state; Use one always @(posedge clk) block to update state and the counter with <=, and a case on state to choose the next state using the decision conditions. Use an assign or an always @(*) block for the outputs. The chart and the code match line by line, which makes reviewing easy.

The digital design flow: Real projects follow a standard flow. 1: Specification, what the system must do, its inputs, outputs and speed. 2: Architecture, splitting into datapath and control, often drawn as block diagrams and ASM charts. 3: HDL coding at register transfer level (RTL). 4: Simulation with testbenches to check functionality. 5: Synthesis, where a tool converts RTL into a netlist of gates and flip-flops from a library, minimising logic much like your K-maps, but automatically. 6: Implementation, placing and routing the gates on an FPGA or chip layout. 7: Timing analysis, checking that every path meets setup and hold times at the target clock. 8: Programming the FPGA or sending the chip for fabrication, and finally testing the real hardware.

Real life example 1, a student project: A final-year team at a Dhaka university wants a digital voting machine for a class election. They write the specification: four candidate buttons, a lock after each vote, a count per candidate, and a result display. They draw an ASM chart for the control: idle, vote received, lock, wait for officer reset. They write Verilog modules for the counters and the 7-segment decoders, test them in a simulator, then load the design onto an FPGA board. Every topic in this course appears in one small project.

Real life example 2, chip design jobs: Bangladesh has a growing semiconductor design sector, with companies and design centres in Dhaka doing physical design and verification for international chip firms. Engineers there spend their days reading and writing HDL, writing testbenches, running synthesis and timing analysis. The gates, flip-flops, counters and state machines you learned are exactly the things those tools generate and check.

Course recap, part 1, combinational: We started with digital signals and number systems, binary arithmetic and complements, and codes like BCD, Gray and parity. Then gates and Boolean algebra, canonical forms, K-maps, don't-cares and the Quine-McCluskey method to simplify logic. We implemented logic with NAND and NOR, and designed real combinational blocks: code converters, adders and subtractors, carry lookahead, BCD adders, multipliers, comparators, decoders, encoders, multiplexers, and we learned how hazards and delays cause glitches.

Course recap, part 2, sequential and beyond: Then we added memory: latches, flip-flops with their characteristic and excitation tables, analysis and design of clocked sequential circuits with Mealy and Moore models, registers and shift registers, and counters. We saw memory and programmable logic from ROM and PLA to FPGA, real logic families, and finally HDL and ASM charts that tie everything together. Next courses that build on this one are computer architecture, microprocessors and embedded systems, and VLSI design.

Common mistakes: In Verilog, students mix = and <= and get simulations that do not match the hardware. They forget the default branch in case statements and create latches by accident. In ASM charts, students treat each box as a separate clock cycle; remember, one whole ASM block is one cycle, and conditional outputs belong to the state above them. Also, delays like #10 do not synthesise; they are only for testbenches.

What exams ask: "Write Verilog for a full adder using assign", "Write a behavioural Verilog model of a D flip-flop or a 4-bit counter", "Explain blocking and nonblocking assignments", "Draw the symbols of an ASM chart and explain an ASM block", "Draw an ASM chart for a given controller and derive its state table", "Describe the steps of the digital design flow".

Recap: HDLs like Verilog describe hardware in text for simulation and synthesis. A module has ports and a body; assign describes combinational logic; always @(*) with = also builds combinational logic; always @(posedge clk) with <= builds flip-flops. ASM charts use state boxes, decision boxes and conditional output boxes, and one ASM block is one clock cycle. The design flow runs from specification through RTL, simulation, synthesis, implementation and timing analysis to real hardware. You now have the full toolkit of digital logic design.
key_points: An HDL (Verilog, VHDL) describes hardware in text for simulation and synthesis; statements run concurrently.
A Verilog module has a name, ports and a body; assign describes combinational logic, e.g. assign s = a ^ b;
always @(*) with = for combinational logic; always @(posedge clk) with <= for flip-flops and registers.
Nonblocking <= updates all registers together at the clock edge, so shift registers work correctly.
ASM chart: state box (Moore outputs), decision box, conditional output box (Mealy outputs).
One ASM block (a state box plus its decisions and conditional boxes) equals one clock cycle.
Design flow: specification, architecture, RTL coding, simulation, synthesis, implementation, timing analysis, hardware test.
lessons.tip: For every Verilog block you write, first say aloud whether it is combinational or sequential. Combinational: always @(*) and =. Sequential: always @(posedge clk) and <=. This one habit prevents most beginner bugs.
lessons.task: On paper, write a Verilog module for a 2-to-1 multiplexer using assign y = sel ? b : a; and a module for a 3-bit up counter with reset using always @(posedge clk). Then draw an ASM chart for a machine that turns on a light for one clock cycle each time a button input goes from 0 to 1.
